World.title: Sophie Cunningham vs DiJonai Carrington: How two ex-football players collided in the 'privilege' debate
World.content:
It was one dreaded moment after another for the WNBA.

Months of conflict came to a breaking point Saturday when DiJonai Carrington struck Sophie Cunningham in the face. A scuffle ensued, Carrington was ejected and then came the social media post that lit the internet on fire.

"White privilege."

DIJONAI CARRINGTON DECLARES 'WHITE PRIVILEGE' AFTER EJECTION FOR SMACKING SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM IN THE FACE

And just like that, the WNBA discourse was about race again. Not just sex, as it had been for weeks.

The hit was a product of two different players from two different worlds, but with novel similarities.

Cunningham and Carrington both played football, but in very different settings

The WNBA's infamous hit just so happened to involve two former football players that played against boys.

Carrington played two years of flag football and then two years of tackle during her elementary school years. She wanted to play because her brother and sister played it too.

Growing up in San Diego, Carrington's father Darren Carrington played for five different NFL teams, but they called San Diego home.

Her father's career earnings are not known, but based on the averages of NFL salaries at the time, he likely made multiple millions of dollars across his eight-year career. DiJonai attended the private Horizon Christian Academy, where her mother was her basketball coach coach.

On the first day of 2015, DiJonai penned an essay that was published in ESPN.com about flying out to California to watch her brother, Darren Jr., play in the Rose Bowl.

Meanwhile, Cunningham went to public high school in Columbia, Missouri. But she attended a private Catholic school during her younger years.

Cunningham played football at Rock Bridge High School with grown boys, but didn't do any tackling like Carrington did in elementary school.

Cunningham was a placekicker, and was protected from any plays that involved tackling, but she still made school history as the first girl to score varsity points.

She grew up on a 2,500 acre farm, and once suggested she came from a "blue-collar" background.

"I would never speak down upon middle class, blue-collar working people. That's where I come from," Cunningham said last July, in an apology for criticizing the selection of Cleveland as a WNBA expansion city.

Her maternal family operated a large farm while her father worked as a building contractor, but things changed for the Cunningham family in 2008.

Cunningham revealed in a July interview on the "Sons and Daughters" podcast, that the 2008 financial crisis impacted her family.

"We were raised in a really good family who gave us more than what we could think of. But that doesn't mean that we didn't have hard times. Our dad was a contractor in the 2008 Economic [crisis], all that stuff that hit our family very hard. And when I say very hard, very very hard," she said.

"And so people look at me and it's really easy to be like 'Oh, she had everything' or 'She did whatever.' It's like, no, we went through some hard times as a family. But honestly, looking back, those were our most fun times. Like we were in a smaller house. We were together 24/7. There were no extra rooms to go to. Some people could be embarrassed by that, but I take great pride like 'Hey, our family isn't built on fluff and all the shiny and crazy things. We have a real family that when hard times hit, they're going to show you even more love than you knew existed."

Cunningham stayed close to home for college, Carrington went on a journey

Both were nationally ranked recruits. Both became McDonald's All-Americans. Both played AAU basketball, which put them in front of college coaches beyond their hometowns.

But Cunningham's recruitment was practically over before she entered high school.

After eighth grade, Cunningham joined the Missouri Eclipse on the AAU circuit. Missouri coach Robin Pingeton began recruiting both Sophie and her older sister Lindsey, eventually offering each a full scholarship.

The sisters committed to Missouri, even as Cunningham's reputation grew and other coaches continued calling.

The decision kept her close to home, but it also continued a family tradition. Her mother, father, aunt, uncle and grandfather had all competed for Missouri.

And Sophie immediately became the face of the program.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

In her fourth college game, she scored a school-record 42 points against Wake Forest. She was named SEC Freshman of the Year and helped Missouri reach the NCAA Tournament for the first time in a decade.

The Tigers made the tournament in all four of her seasons.

By the end of her career, Cunningham was a three-time First-Team All-SEC selection and a Third-Team All-American. She finished as Missouri's all-time leading scorer with 2,187 points and also set the school record for free throws made.

Carrington took a longer winding road through college.

Two ACL surgeries limited her to two and a half seasons of high school basketball. But she still scored more than 2,000 points, played for Cal Sparks Gold on the club circuit and became a five-star recruit.

She first committed to Stanford, the famed elite university on the West Coast.

Carrington came off the bench as a freshman for a team that reached the Final Four and won the Pac-12 Tournament. Two years later, she became a full-time starter and averaged 14 points and 7.5 rebounds.

She was named All-Pac-12 and helped Stanford win another conference tournament title before reaching the Elite Eight.

Then her knee interrupted her career again.

Carrington played just five games during her senior season before another injury forced her out. She still graduated from Stanford with two undergraduate degrees, one in psychology and another in African and African American studies.

She also received a medical hardship waiver, giving her another year of eligibility.

So while Cunningham spent her entire college career in the city where she was raised, Carrington entered the transfer portal and started another recruiting process during the COVID-19 shutdown.

Carrington ended up going to Baylor, and started only one game there. But she became the team's second-leading scorer with 14.1 points per game. She was named both the Big 12 Newcomer of the Year and Sixth Player of the Year.

Baylor won the Big 12 regular-season and tournament championships before losing to UConn by two points in the Elite Eight.

Cunningham and Carrington have since become symbols for two different sides of the WNBA

Both players entered the WNBA as second-round picks.

Cunningham went 13th overall (first pick of the second round) to the Phoenix Mercury in 2019. Carrington went 20th (eighth pick of the second round) to the Connecticut Sun two years later in 2021.

Cunningham spent six seasons in Phoenix, where she developed the "Spicy Sophie" nickname and a reputation for playing with emotion. She was a shooter, an agitator and a willing participant in almost any confrontation.

Carrington spent four seasons in Connecticut and built a similar reputation from the defensive side of the ball.

She went from a reserve to one of the league's most disruptive perimeter defenders. In 2024, Carrington was named the WNBA's Most Improved Player and made the All-Defensive First Team.

But their reputations eventually became bigger than their performances.

Cunningham was traded to Indiana before the 2025 season, placing her alongside Caitlin Clark and in front of the largest audience in the league.

Her popularity exploded in June when she committed a hard foul on Connecticut's Jacy Sheldon after Sheldon made contact with Clark's eye. Cunningham was ejected, but many Fever fans celebrated the foul as an act of protection.

Then came Cunningham's label: "The Enforcer."

Cunningham leaned into her bold personality through fashion, social media and a podcast she launched with longtime friend and reality television personality West Wilson.

Her romantic life, however, has remained mostly private.

Cunningham has not publicly identified a current partner. On her podcast, she said she has only dated older men and discussed wanting to eventually get married and have children.

"I want to get married and I want to have a family," Cunningham said in October.

Carrington's relationship was much more public.

She began dating NaLyssa Smith after the two played together at Baylor. Their on-and-off relationship continued after both entered the WNBA, with fans following the couple through social media posts, vacations and courtside appearances.

Carrington resisted putting a label on her sexuality.

"I'm not gay, I just like Lyss," she said in 2025.

Their careers brought them together again in Dallas in 2025, when Carrington was traded to the Wings and Smith arrived from Indiana.

It lasted only a few months.

Dallas traded Smith to Las Vegas in June, leaving Smith "sick to my stomach" about being unexpectedly separated from Carrington, according to a social media post she made after the deal.

Carrington was later traded to Minnesota in August 2025. But by November, the relationship was over.

Carrington initially said the two remained on good terms but had grown in different directions. Then, in July 2026, she publicly accused Smith of cheating on her with other WNBA players.

Smith questioned why Carrington brought the allegations forward after their breakup and disputed Carrington's portrayal of the surrounding events, but did not directly confirm or deny the accusation.

One of the WNBA's most visible romances had become part of the league's public drama.

The two players also became political symbols.

Carrington has repeatedly spoken about racial justice, gender equality and the treatment of Black women. She has connected that advocacy to the African and African American studies education she received at Stanford.

"I'll never back down from a conversation or from standing up for what I know is right," Carrington said in 2025.

That outspokenness made her popular with some WNBA fans and a villain to others.

During the 2024 playoffs, Carrington accidentally struck Clark near the eye while attempting to block a pass. Clark said she did not believe it was intentional, but Carrington still received racist messages, sexual threats and death threats.

Cunningham became a political figure from the opposite direction.

In 2026, she voiced support for excluding transgender girls and women from female sports. The comments attracted praise from conservative figures and protests outside Fever games.

Cunningham said she would not hide her beliefs simply because others disagreed.

The controversy transformed her from a popular role player into one of the most polarizing athletes in the league.

Meanwhile, Carrington signed with Chicago while recovering from her foot injury. She returned to the court in late July 2026 after missing the first half of the season.

Cunningham returned to Indiana after recovering from the knee injury that ended her 2025 season.

By the time the two collided on Aug. 8, neither was viewed as just another WNBA player.

Cunningham was the white, heterosexual, Christian enforcer who had become a conservative symbol.

Carrington was the Black activist and former half of one of the league's most visible same-sex relationships.

So when Carrington hit Cunningham, the public did not see only a foul.

It saw everything the two women had come to represent.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

And when Carrington made her "White privilege" post, it cemented the whole thing as a potential defining moment in WNBA history, or at least this current volatile chapter.

Carrington later insisted her post was not about the officials’ decision. "I never once claimed that the assessment of the foul was white privilege," she wrote Monday. She said "I would never use that term as a rhetorical weapon knowing the historical and social weight it holds without having the proper evidence to substantiate it."

Still, she's remained vague about what she meant.

World.title: JCB Hydromax shatters a world record with ‘extraordinary’ speeds topping 400 mph in hydrogen-powered car
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

There is fast, and then there is what JCB Hydromax achieved with its hydrogen-powered car Tuesday.

The twin-engined, 32-foot car completed two runs at the Bonneville Salt Flats, recording an average speed of 400.623 mph in its first run, and going 412.135 mph on its second run.

The average speed of 406.320 mph set the world land speed record and is the fastest a hydrogen-powered internal combustion car has ever traveled, shattering the previous mark of 185.5 mph set by the BMW H2R in 2004.

The record is subject to official confirmation by the Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile (FIA).

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Wing Commander Andy Green, who drove the car, called the record an "extraordinary" engineering achievement.

"This is the first of a new breed. They have created a new class at Bonneville Speed Week for hydrogen racing, the internal combustion engine. And it's not only a new class, but it's also blown every other hydrogen car out of the water with this record," Green told Fox News Digital in a recent interview.

Green said the process to get a car up to 400 mph normally takes about three to five years. JCB Hydromax had its first design meeting just over a year ago.

"JCB, by comparison, just over a year ago, sat down for their first design meeting with their project team to work out how they were going to do this," Green said.

"They had nine months to design and manufacture components. They built the car in five weeks, tested it for three weeks in the U.K. and then came straight to Bonneville with the aim of setting a record on their first visit in a brand new car using new technology, which these hydrogen engines they're running.

"They were running them at a perfect fuel ratio, which no one had ever built for a hydrogen engine. This is unique technology."

Green said the professionals who do this year in and year out thought it would take a few visits over five or six years to achieve the feat.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

"Instead of five or six years, they did it in five or six days," Green said.

The esteemed driver praised the team’s work in putting it together considering the process of achieving 400 mph is an arduous one.

Engine development presented plenty of problems for the engineers to work around, including being 6,000 to 7,000 feet above sea level and dealing with temperatures of 100 to 105 degrees at the Bonneville Salt Flats.

Packaging such a high-energy engine output in a small space also creates cooling problems. To combat that, the car was equipped with about 400 pounds of ice and water to cool not only the engines but also the air being sucked in and turbocharged.

The hydrogen engines cannot run with hot air, because, with hot air, the hydrogen "will go bang straight away."

"It’s a small angry molecule that loves to burn," Green said.

However, if the water seeps into the crevices of the engine and mixes with the engine oil, it will destroy the bearings and the engine in just a few seconds.

To counteract that, the oil needs to be heated so that when the water inevitably hits it, the water will boil and evaporate right away. Yet, the oil can’t be so hot that it is overheated.

After about a week of testing, it was determined the oil needed to be heated to about 180 degrees Fahrenheit.

Just as important as hitting top speed is making sure the car stops safely. The parachute system is paramount to slowing the car safely and is unique to the car. It plays a massive role in slowing down a 5,500-pound car going 400 mph.

After ensuring everything was correct, Green said the team got the exact result it was looking for.

"All of those things came together. Today, we went away from Wendover towards Salt Lake City," Green said. "It had done an average through the measured mile of 400 miles an hour. It's exactly what we were aiming for as a minimum. Then did the full turnaround."

After doing a full body check and replacing the tires because they get exceptionally hot at those speeds, the team felt confident about pushing the car a little further because everything went so well on the first run.

"This is the most power we've ever run, the most speed we've ever run. Eased up another 20 mph. We got, I think it was 412 miles an hour the other way. An average, which,subject to confirmation, is a new world record for a hydrogen car, 406 mph. Absolutely amazing achievement," Green said.

The time it took to complete the measured mile was just under nine seconds. The track is 105 feet wide, and Green said he was gently steering the "beast" of a car down the track.

"You can do 70 to 80 miles an hour on the interstate. So, it's five or six times faster than that. It's fast. It has the weird effect that the track is 105 feet wide, and there's marker boards a quarter mile down each side. So, the marker boards as you're looking in the distance at the marker boards, and they come to get at you about a second away or two seconds away. But as you accelerate, you need to look further and further and further in the distance," Green said.

"The marker boards that you're looking at now are much, much closer together and coming at you much faster. It actually makes the track look narrower and narrower and narrower as you go faster. It's quite a weird visual effect, but it's very powerful."

On the second run, Green was more concerned about slowing down the car because the faster it went, the longer it took to stop.

"And, on both occasions, the car stopped right there into the track exactly as we planned," Green said.

For Green, going fast is common. He discovered the world of driving at supersonic speeds through a press release, and his day job gave him the perfect background for it.

"I've been lucky enough to have as a career working in the military as a jet fighter pilot in the U.K., in the Royal Air Force. So, world's best day job flying jet fighters," Green said.

"I don't pretend to be Tom Cruise. Tom Cruise pretends to be me. It's that kind of job. It's one of those, ‘Do they really pay me to do this?’ It's fantastic."

So, when Green saw a press launch for a new project for the land-speed record, he thought with his background he’d be perfect for the task.

"(In) college, I did math, that was very much my thing, so I'm very much into the science of how these things work. And then, since then, I've been flying supersonic vehicles, and I look at this, and that's not really a racing driver's job. Not at those speeds, that's more, ‘Where are you going to get somebody that is qualified to understand and drive a supersonic vehicle powered by jet engines?’ That would be my day job," Green said.

"The more I looked at it, the more fascinating a technical challenge it became to work out how we were going to do this."

In 1997, Green set the world land-speed record, reaching 763.035 mph, and became the first and only person to break the sound barrier on land. The record still stands today.

What makes Green excited is that today’s technology is the beginning of a new era in motorsport.

"It's actually showcasing the genuine zero-carbon technology of the future," Green said.

"This is, you know, you can make hydrogen from sunlight and water, put it in a race car and do 400 miles an hour. That's an exciting future for motorsport."

World.title: White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt to step down
World.content:
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt will be leaving the administration at the end of the month, after serving in the role since the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term.

Trump on Wednesday announced that Leavitt, 28, the youngest White House press secretary, is set to step down to “spend more time with her beautiful young children and family.”

“Karoline will now be one of my top outside advisors, and an influential voice within the Republican Party, as we work to defy History, and conclusively win the Midterm Elections,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt speaks with reporters in the James Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House on July 23. Julia Demaree Nikhinson / AP file

Leavitt, who gave birth to her second child in May, making her the first White House press secretary to have a child while serving in the role, confirmed her departure in a statement on X.

She said that being called press secretary has been “the honor and adventure of a lifetime,” adding that since having her second child, she “felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary.”

Leavitt returned to the podium from maternity leave on July 16.

“I am thankful to the President for entrusting me with the distinct privilege of speaking on his behalf at the White House podium,” said Leavitt, who is one of only eight women to have served in the role.

Neither Trump nor Leavitt indicated in their social media posts who might be named the next White House press secretary.

During her maternity leave, the White House did not name an interim press secretary, instead opting to have various administration officials brief the news media. Those officials included Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

Leavitt was an assistant White House press secretary during Trump’s first term. She later became national press secretary during his 2024 presidential campaign.

Leavitt gave birth to her first child during the 2024 presidential campaign, returning to work just four days into her maternity leave after the assassination attempt on Trump in Butler, Pennsylvania.

Earlier this year, Leavitt had intended for her April 24 press briefing to be the last one before she went on leave. But she unexpectedly returned to hold a briefing shortly after the April 25 shooting at the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner.

Leavitt is the fifth woman in a high-ranking position to leave the Trump administration this year, following the departures of Pam Bondi as attorney general, Kristi Noem as homeland security secretary, Lori Chavez-DeRemer as labor secretary and Tulsi Gabbard as director of national intelligence. All four have been replaced by men.

At a little over 18 months, Leavitt’s tenure is the second-longest for a White House press secretary under Trump. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, who’s now governor of Arkansas, was in the role for nearly two years during Trump’s first term. None of Trump’s other press secretaries — Sean Spicer, Stephanie Grisham and Kayleigh McEnany — lasted a full year in the job.

In between Trump’s two terms, Leavitt made an unsuccessful bid for Congress. She ran for a House seat in New Hampshire in 2022 and lost to Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas.

World.title: Nick Reiner pleads not guilty to murder charges in stabbing deaths of parents Rob and Michele Reiner
World.content:
Nick Reiner has been indicted on murder charges in the deaths of his parents, Rob and Michele Reiner, in a stabbing attack inside the family’s Brentwood home in December.

He pleaded not guilty Wednesday to two counts of murder, with special circumstance allegations of multiple murders and murder by means of lying in wait, according to Los Angeles County officials.

Nick Reiner during his arraignment on murder charges for the deaths of his parents on Feb. 23, 2026, in Los Angeles. Chris Torres / Pool via AP file

Reiner, 32, was brought to a 13th-floor courtroom at the Criminal Courts Building, in downtown Los Angeles, to answer to the new charges, which will replace the original murder case filed in 2025. The indictment, which was returned last month, adds a special circumstance allegation of lying in wait.

Special circumstances allegations can increase potential penalties in the sentencing phase of a trial.

“This was a profound betrayal by someone who was loved and trusted by the very people he is accused of killing,” Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan J. Hochman said in a statement Wednesday.

His appointed defense attorney, L.A. Deputy Public Defender Kimberly Greene, declined to comment following the arraignment.

The indictment speeds the case toward a jury trial, bypassing the need for a public preliminary hearing, which had been expected to take place sometime in the fall.

From left, Rob Reiner, Michele Singer Reiner, Romy Reiner and Nick Reiner on Sept. 9, 2025, in Los Angeles. Richard Shotwell / Invision / AP

He also faces a special allegation that he personally used a dangerous and deadly weapon, a knife, the DA said.

Reiner, who is being held without bail, was arrested Dec. 15, a day after his parents’ bodies were discovered in their bedroom. He is scheduled to return to court for a hearing on Sept. 15.

If convicted, Reiner faces death or life in state prison without the possibility of parole. The DA said a decision on whether to seek the death penalty will be made at a later date.

The deaths of Rob Reiner, 78, a celebrated director whose long list of films included “When Harry Met Sally…,” “A Few Good Men” and “This Is Spinal Tap,” and Michele Reiner, 70, a photographer and producer, stunned the Hollywood community and led to an outpouring of tributes from entertainment industry colleagues, political figures and more. The family’s challenges with Nick, including battles with drug addiction, were well-documented.

In September, the family appeared together at the Los Angeles premiere of “Spinal Tap 2: The End Continues.”

Nick Reiner has spoken publicly over the years about his struggles with drug addiction, which began in his teens. He told People in an interview in 2016 that he cycled in and out of treatment facilities with bouts of homelessness and relapses in between.

World.title: Two people are dead after a military helicopter crashes in Texas, sparking a fire
World.content:
Two people who were on board a military helicopter were killed Wednesday when it crashed in Salado, Texas, the Bell County Sheriff’s Office said.

They were pronounced dead after officials responded to 911 calls around 1:30 p.m., said Cliff Coleman of the Bell County Sheriff’s Office. Salado is about 50 miles north of Austin.

The AH-64 U.S. Army Apache attack helicopter is based at Fort Hood, the military installation said.

“Our immediate priority is securing the site and supporting the initial response efforts,” Brig. Gen. Ethan Diven, acting commanding general, said in a statement. “Our thoughts are with the crew and their families as we await further information.”

The victims have not yet been publicly identified.

The scene of a helicopter crash in Salado, Texas on Wednesday. Bell County Sheriff’s Office

No structures were damaged, and no other injuries were reported, Coleman said.

“It crashed into a field, and you could tell it was a violent crash,” Coleman told reporters on scene.

The crash caused a large fire that “looks to be out of control,” he said. It has led to a large area of land being burned and has prompted some evacuations in the area.

Local emergency responders, military personnel and law enforcement all responded to the incident. The criminal investigation division of Fort Hood is leading the inquiry.

The AH-64 Apache helicopter is a twin-engine, four-bladed, multi-mission attack helicopter designed as a highly stable aerial weapons-delivery platform, the Army said on its website, calling it “the most advanced aerial fighting vehicle in the world.”

World.title: Extremism expert charged in case on Southern Poverty Law Center informants
World.content:
A former official at the Southern Poverty Law Center is now facing federal charges in connection with a case the Justice Department brought over the way the organization made payments to informants who provided details on extremist organizations.

Heidi Beirich has been charged in federal court in Montgomery, Alabama, her attorney said. Attorney General Todd Blanche said at an unrelated press conference on Wednesday that the case involved allegations Beirich “was part of the effort to open bank accounts and completely fictitious companies’ names and make payments that to individuals for reasons that were not that were not accurate as as described.” CNN first reported on the charges against Beirich.

“A free and fair society does not use the justice system to silence its political opponents,” Beirich attorney Michael J. Proctor said in a statement. “Heidi Beirich has dedicated her life to fighting hate groups and extremist movements like the KKK, neo-Nazis, and other white supremacists. She has combatted these hateful, ugly, and un-American extremists and their repeated uses of violence and intimidation in order to promote a fairer, safer, and more just America. Her decades-long record of success dismantling hate groups—and the resulting threats to her life—speak volumes. For this, she has been indicted.”

Beirich is the former chief financial officer at the Southern Poverty Law Center. The indictment alleges that Beirich “was in a romantic relationship” with one informant who infiltrated the National Alliance, a neo-Nazi organization, and was paid more than $1.2 million over the court of several years.

The charges were a part of the Justice Department’s effort to prosecute the nonprofit over the alleged payments, which prosecutors say were done through shell companies, without the knowledge of donors.

But the Southern Povery Law Center said that federal authorities were aware of the organization’s use of informants, mischaracterized the program and that the Trump administration is targeting the group because of its politics. The group said the government has used information gathered by its informants in the past.

The nonprofit civil rights organization was founded in 1971 and is based in Montgomery, Ala. It initially focused on the enforcement of civil rights laws in the South, but has expanded over time. The group has been a frequent target of attacks by conservative critics who claim the nonprofit is politically biased.

U.S. District Judge Emily Marks declined to dismiss the case against the SPLC, ruling last week that the SPLC had failed to provide objective evidence to show that the group was being targeted by the Justice Department for exercising its First Amendment rights.

Abbe Lowell, an attorney representing the SPLC, said the Beirich case is “as legally and factually flawed as their previous attacks” and reflected “a desperate government confronting a weak case, scrambling to make something – anything - stick as we approach trial.”

The SPLC, Lowell said, “did not lie to donors, did not mislead the banks it did business with, and its informant program prevented violence and saved lives.”

World.title: Zhu Rongji, who drove China's 1990s economic reforms, has died at 97
World.content:
Zhu Rongji, who drove China's 1990s economic reforms, has died at 97

Enlarge this image toggle caption K.Y. Cheng/South China Morning Post via Getty Images K.Y. Cheng/South China Morning Post via Getty Images

Zhu Rongji, former premier of China, has died at age 97. The cause of death was given as illness, according to state media.

Zhu, an acerbic technocrat and a trained engineer, was renowned for far-reaching economic reforms throughout the 1990s that sought to transition China from the chaos of its post-Maoist years to a more global market-oriented financial system, without completely ceding the Communist Party's control over the economy.

Despite staying almost completely out of the public eye after retiring from the premiership in 2003, he remains a polarizing figure in the country indelibly shaped by him. His reform legacy remains contested in China; in freeing up the country's enormous labor and financial resources, he helped to create vast amounts of wealth over the next three decades while also seeding institutions with future vulnerabilities.

Sponsor Message

"From the point of view of a policymaker, [he] embraced the notion of a China whose economic system was more compatible with that of the West. And by compatible, I mean vastly reformed, more open, less state-dominated, very limited state intervention," said Charlene Barshefsky, a lawyer and former U.S. trade representative who sat across the negotiating table from Zhu over years-long talks to let China enter the World Trade Organization (WTO).

In order to join the WTO, China first needed to get preferential trading status with the United States — which in turn demanded hard concessions and that it open up its closed economy to American companies. Zhu was under huge pressure to find compromise, and he let his views be known.

Enlarge this image toggle caption Joyce Naltchayan/AFP via Getty Images Joyce Naltchayan/AFP via Getty Images

In 2000, the U.S. Senate voted to give China that preferential trading status, and the following year, China joined the WTO. The agreement was a windfall for the nascent Chinese economy. The country became an export powerhouse, and foreign businesses rushed to China to establish a foothold.

The 6 1/2-year process let Zhu show off his flinty personality, though he struck U.S. officials as inquisitive and flexible. "This was not talking points. It was a lot of give and take," said Kenneth Lieberthal, a China expert who was a national security adviser for then-President Bill Clinton. He met Zhu multiple times during the negotiations.

Sponsor Message

Zhu was born in 1928 in the city of Changsha, in China's Hunan province. He graduated from Beijing's Tsinghua University, where he was also chosen as president of the student union, with a degree in electrical engineering, the winter before the Communist Party won control over China. In October 1949, when the new Communist-led republic was founded, Zhu officially joined the Chinese Communist Party.

His blunt, say-it-like-it-is style got him in trouble

Zhu's father died before he was born, and his mother died when he was 9 years old. Being an orphan, the need to survive helped shape his strong personality: thick-skinned and extremely direct.

"My defining characteristic is independent thought," he told bureaucrats in 1987, right before becoming mayor of Shanghai. "I say what I think."

When Chinese troops fatally fired on pro-democracy protesters in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989, Zhu did not issue the standard propaganda line denying the tragedy. "The event that occurred recently in Beijing is a historical fact, and historical facts cannot be covered up by anybody. The truth will always come out," he wrote in an essay published in a Shanghai newspaper.

His blunt, say-it-like-it-is style got him in serious trouble. In 1958, he was labeled an ideological "rightist" and briefly expelled from the party for criticizing Chairman Mao Zedong's economic policies, but managed to hold on to a job in state planning. In 1970, he was purged again during the Cultural Revolution and sent to do five years of manual labor at a party reeducation school.

Zhu was rehabilitated after Mao died in 1976 and Deng Xiaoping came to power as China's leader. Zhu then worked his way back up the bureaucratic ladder with the same pragmatism he had learned as an engineer.

"Regardless of what country your company is from, when you arrive in China, you should receive fair and equal treatment. I just want you to pay taxes," he joked in 1999 to an audience of American businessmen, explaining that China was open for foreign investment.

Sponsor Message

A career state planner, Zhu nevertheless quickly adjusted to the economic chaos of the 1990s, as China careened between capitalism and state-led socialism. As central bank governor, Zhu successfully tamed runaway inflation. While vice premier, he also led a dramatic centralization of the tax system that incentivized land sales and huge wealth creation, along with hugely unsustainable levels of debt.

After being appointed premier in 1998, he entered office with a bold promise: He would reform the indebted state banks within two years and inefficient state enterprises within three. That earned him both instant enemies and fans.

"No matter whether what lies ahead is a minefield or a bottomless abyss, I will carry out my duties until the last breath in my body," he vowed.

Zhu's most controversial legacy by far remains restructuring China's bloated state-owned enterprises. He axed smaller, inefficient companies, leaving an estimated 30 million state workers suddenly jobless.

Worker protests erupted all over China. Zhu had the willpower — or callousness, as his critics would say — to ignore them.

"The central government decided that the laid-off worker problem could just be ignored and forgotten," said Dorothy Solinger, a professor emeritus of political science at the University of California, Irvine, who studies migrant labor in China.

Zhu tried to offset the layoffs' impacts. He created a basic social welfare system that exists to this day and made steps to boost basic health care, which had crumbled in rural areas. But pockets of China, especially in the northeast region of the country, where workers were reliant on state employment in heavy industry sectors, never fully recovered economically.

"I think their children also have a problem because they miss out on the things that the better-off part of the population could do, such as hiring tutors or going on extracurricular activities, going to the better schools," said Solinger. "It's a growing underclass."

Sponsor Message

Zhu took the criticism in stride. Unlike most Communist leaders, who read off staid and carefully prepared scripts, he loved engaging with and ad-libbing to the press.

"He loved answering all the questions, no matter how tough or sensitive," remembered Rose Luqiu, a former journalist for Hong Kong outlet Phoenix News who spent 10 years covering Zhu during his international state visits. "The only way he refused to answer was using a quite humorous way to dodge the questions."

His gallows humor allowed him to weather intense periods of criticism from senior ideologues within the Communist Party, once quipping during an anti-corruption campaign: "I have prepared 100 coffins: 99 for the corrupt officials and one for myself."

Other reforms of his did not materialize, in part because an austere Zhu never managed to cultivate the political patronage networks that would have allowed him to overcome fierce opposition within party ranks to his proposals. His efforts to reduce bad debt at China's state banks and reform the pension system floundered.

Enlarge this image toggle caption Greg Baker/AFP via Getty Images Greg Baker/AFP via Getty Images

Zhu "represented really a different time, a different era for China"

Zhu is now invoked with pleasant nostalgia. Under China's current leader, Xi Jinping, the country became more nationalistic, more beholden to the state and more closed off to the outside world.

"I think that Zhu Rongji represented really a different time, a different era for China: the time when China wanted to find its way in what, due to that time, was the best possible way, which was to move towards Western-style economics, to move toward Western-style rules," said Barshefsky, the former U.S. trade negotiator.

Zhu Rongji spent the last years of his life at his Beijing home in the western hills of the Chinese capital. He loved Peking Opera and spent much of his days listening to music — and quietly advising some of the newest generation of technocrats running China, though not all appear to have listened to him.

World.title: Canada, U.S. not yet ready to make tariff deal, Canada unsatisfied with latest U.S. offer: sources
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As the clock ticks toward U.S. President Donald Trump's latest tariff deadline, Canada and the U.S. aren't at a point where a tariff deal can be reached — and Canadian officials are not satisfied with the latest U.S. offer, according to two sources with knowledge of the trade talks.

According to sources on both sides of the border, the Americans offered a new proposal on Tuesday which would lower some of the sectoral tariffs but not to the degree that the Canadian side would like to see. CBC News is not naming the sources because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

Negotiators have been going back and forth in recent weeks in an effort to reach some sort of deal before Aug. 19, which is when Trump has promised a 50 per cent levy on hundreds of Canadian goods in addition to the sectoral tariffs already in place.

The Americans are seeking a deal that would see preferential access to Canadian critical minerals and cover security and energy, the sources said.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc has been in Washington to meet with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer three times in as many weeks. CBC News previously reported that the two are aiming to present Trump with a path to a potential trade deal as early as Monday.

Sources told CBC News last week that the Canadian side has aggressively argued to the Americans that there would be no political appetite among Canadians to keep talks going if the Aug. 19 tariffs come into place.

Both sides have agreed to hold daily meetings at various levels up until that deadline, the sources said.

WATCH | New pitch for Trump in the works: Canada-U.S. trade reps working on new pitch for Trump | Duration 2:22 CBC News has learned Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer are working on a proposal to pitch to U.S. President Donald Trump before a tariff deadline that could see hundreds of Canadian goods hit with a 50 per cent levy.

Neither LeBlanc nor Canada's chief trade negotiator, Janice Charette, answered reporters' questions after they were seen leaving Greer's office on Tuesday afternoon.

LeBlanc later posted to X saying that discussions are "ongoing" and he and Charette will "continue to engage at the negotiation table."

LeBlanc's office told CBC News he and Charette remain in Washington as of Wednesday night.

In addition to trying to dissuade Americans from levying new tariffs, LeBlanc and Charette are looking for relief on tariffs the U.S. has slapped on Canadian steel, aluminum, lumber and autos.

Canada is also hoping the ongoing trade talks between the two countries will result in a renewal of the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) after the Trump administration last month declined to extend the deal past 2036.

When announcing the Aug. 19 tariffs, the U.S. raised a number of trade irritants, including Canada's retaliation against U.S. trade policy with the removal of U.S. alcohol from provincial store shelves and alleged Canadian discrimination against U.S. motor vehicles and dairy.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre wrote to Carney on Sunday, calling on him to show some "backbone" as trade negotiations ramp up.

Poilievre said Canadians deserve a "good deal" that includes zero tariffs on softwood lumber, an end to sectoral tariffs on steel and aluminum, a tariff-free auto pact and full exemption to Buy America rules on infrastructure projects at all levels of government.

"No more pursuing policies of a managed decline at home. No more caving," Poilievre wrote.

Industry sources previously told CBC News that Canada is preparing to meet some U.S. demands — including ending the booze bans — in exchange for tariff relief.

World.title: Woman behind petition to oust U.S ambassador says response is 'beyond what I expected'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The woman behind a petition calling for U.S. President Donald Trump's representative in Ottawa to be kicked out of the country says it's grown beyond her expectations.

The online petition, which is set to be presented in the House of Commons in the fall, says Pete Hoekstra should be declared persona non grata and the Canadian government should request his removal as U.S. ambassador to Canada.

More than 70,000 people had signed the petition as of Wednesday evening, approximately double the number of signatures 24 hours earlier.

"It's beyond what I expected out of this," said Lee Walker, the Calgary-based woman behind the petition, in an email to CBC News.

"It tells me that it's not a fringe issue, and that a lot of Canadians are uncomfortable with how Hoekstra has been repeating Trump talking points about our sovereignty and Canada as a whole."

Walker's petition accuses Hoekstra of making statements that undermine the Canada-U.S. diplomatic relationship and of "making repeated interventions in Canadian political discourse inconsistent with diplomatic protocol."

The petition also says Hoekstra has normalized the Trump administration's threats to annex Canada. The ambassador made headlines in June after saying that Canada's annexation by the United States would be a great topic of discussion for Prime Minister Mark Carney and U.S. President Donald Trump.

Walker said comments like that from an ambassador aren't appropriate.

"Words from someone in his position carry immense weight, and normalizing that kind of rhetoric can have real consequences," she said.

Hoekstra has also said it's dangerous for Canadian political leaders to describe the Trump administration's ongoing tariff campaign as a trade war and has criticized Canadian politicians who have responded to the tariffs by discouraging travel to the U.S. and for pulling American liquor off of shelves.

'Turmoil already exists'

The petition also calls on the Liberal government to direct a parliamentary committee to review U.S. diplomatic interference in Canadian affairs.

A spokesperson for the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa declined to comment on the petition except to say the embassy is aware of it.

When asked about the potential impact the petition could have amid sensitive trade talks between the U.S. and Canada, Walker said there's already tension between the two countries.

"The turmoil already exists. It's just one-sided right now," she said.

Walker said her intention is to make clear " that respect for Canada and its sovereignty isn't optional or up for negotiation."

Canadian and American negotiators have been going back and forth in recent weeks in an effort to reach some sort of deal before Aug. 19, which is when Trump has promised a 50 per cent levy on hundreds of Canadian goods in addition to the sectoral tariffs already in place.

WATCH | More about the petition: Canadian petition calls to expel U.S. ambassador | Duration 0:34 Nearly 30,000 Canadians have signed a petition calling for U.S. President Donald Trump's representative in Ottawa to be kicked out of the country. The online petition accuses Ambassador Pete Hoekstra of making statements that undermine the Canada-U.S. diplomatic relationship.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc has been in Washington to meet with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer three times in as many weeks. CBC News previously reported that the two are aiming to present Trump with a path to a potential trade deal as early as Monday.

The petition will be presented in Parliament by Green Party Leader Elizabeth May in the fall. Members of Parliament can table petitions in the House of Commons without endorsing their contents.

As for what she wants to happen once it's presented, Walker said she's not sure the government will take steps to declare Hoekstra persona non grata, but hopes the petition will send a message.

"This sort of conduct from a sitting ambassador isn't something we'll just shrug off," she said.

World.title: New Churchill Falls hydro deal between N.L. and Quebec being finalized: sources
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Quebec and Newfoundland Labrador are close to a new deal on Churchill Falls, sources with knowledge of the matter have confirmed to CBC News.

The sources were not authorized to speak publicly.

They said two or three issues are outstanding but are close to being resolved and the two governments are aiming to make a formal announcement early next week.

Montreal-based newspaper, La Presse, has reported that an agreement has been reached.

A spokesperson from the N.L. premier's office said, however, that "As of right now, no final deal has been signed."

"We can confirm that in recent days we have made significant progress in our negotiations with both Quebec and the Government of Canada as it relates to replacing the 2024 MOU with a new deal for Churchill Falls and Gull Island," said Ashley Politi, a spokesperson for Tony Wakeham.

Meanwhile, a spokesperson for Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette said in French that she can "neither confirm nor deny this information at the moment."

The development comes just weeks after Wakeham and Fréchette met in Prince Edward Island to discuss a new agreement for the sale and development of Churchill Falls power.

Liberal former premier Andrew Furey initially signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Quebec — aimed at ending and replacing the controversial 1969 Churchill Falls contract — in Dec. of 2024.

The deal also promised the development of Gull Island, a long-discussed hydroelectric project also located on the Churchill River.

That MOU was expected to be formalized by April 2026 — but this never happened.

After the October 2025 provincial election, the new Progressive Conservative government called for an independent review of the MOU by a committee. In the spring, that committee concluded that the MOU was not in the public interest.

During the election, Wakeham also promised that the Churchill Falls MOU would be put to a referendum. But he has been tight lipped since — only stating that a deal needs to be made first.

Negotiations between N.L. and Quebec resumed in June.

Wakeham needs to be transparent, opposition says

Meanwhile, the opposition Liberals are expressing frustration with how the information has been released to the public.

"Once again, Newfoundlanders and Labradorians are learning about the latest MOU developments through Quebec media rather than from our own government," an emailed statement from the opposition said.

"They’re reporting that a new deal has been reached, but that the core of the agreement remains similar to the previous MOU. Premier Wakeham needs to be transparent with Newfoundlanders and Labradorians."

World.title: Why this American doctor is leaving Utah to serve a remote community in B.C.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

American physician Leo Bay and his family are busy boxing up their belongings and getting ready to leave their home in Utah.

"It's a big move, but it's an exciting move," Bay said.

They've decided to move to Canada where Bay will work as a family doctor on the Sunshine Coast.

When he, his wife and their three children first got off the ferry to visit Pender Harbour, they knew instantly it was where they wanted to live.

"We fell in love with the Sunshine Coast," Bay said.

The Bay family has been living in a rural area of Utah and believes the transition to the Sunshine Coast should be smooth as they enjoy the outdoors. (Pender Harbour Health Centre)

Bay has been practising medicine for eight years and has worked with remote communities as the associate chief medical information officer for Wisconsin, Minnesota, and North Dakota.

At the end of August, he starts at the Pender Harbour Health Centre providing care to 1,000 people in the remote B.C. coastal community.

"The opportunity to be able to live and work in that community is so exciting and so meaningful," Bay said.

Why Canada?

Bay said he's looking forward to focusing on patient care.

"I think that there are lots of things within the U.S. health system that as a primary care doctor we struggle with," he said. "Insurances in the U.S. only cover very limited portions of things or have very strict restrictions."

The idea of coming to Canada five years ago would have been disruptive, he said, and felt impossible.

B.C.’s Ministry of Health said that more than 2,900 job applications have been received from U.S. health-care workers and physicians as of March 2026. (Pender Harbour Health Centre)

Back in July 2025, the College of Physicians and Surgeons of B.C. implemented bylaw changes that help U.S.-trained doctors become fully licensed in B.C. without the need for further assessment, examination or training if they hold certification from the American Board of Medical Specialties, American Board of Family Medicine or the American Osteopathic Board of Family Physicians.

B.C.'s Ministry of Health launched a $5-million digital advertising blitz in June 2025, targeting health workers in Washington state, Oregon and California. Ads have also been running in U.S. academic publications through September.

"Seeing the programs that were available, that really made a difference in making it feel like something that was feasible," Bay said.

Nick Gaskin, executive director at the Pender Harbour Health Centre, said a community member donated $105,000 to the clinic so renovations could be done, which he said helped bring in the new American doctors. (Pender Harbour Health Centre)

According to the Ministry of Health, more than 580 U.S. health-care workers, including 270 physicians, have accepted job offers in communities throughout B.C. as of March 2026.

"B.C. now has the most doctors per capita in Canada with more than 15,000 physicians, an increase of 23 per cent from 2017 to 2024," said the ministry.

4 new doctors to Sunshine Coast

At the Pender Harbour Health Centre, Bay will be in the company of a fellow American who also moved to Canada.

Dr. Derek Williams, who has been practising medicine for 25 years, moved from Montana earlier this year.

Nick Gaskin, executive director at the centre, said they only had one part-time physician serving 500 people before the two new physicians joined.

Pender Harbour Health Centre recently underwent a $300,000 renovation to the primary care wing that was made possible through donations from the community, according to Gaskin. (Pender Harbour Health Centre)

"To have 2,000 members of our community attached to physicians at this clinic is going to be fantastic," Gaskin said.

The remote nature of the community has posed a challenge to attract and retain physicians over the years, he said.

"I think the political landscape certainly makes a difference. I also think that we live in a different world right now where people are moving around," Gaskin said.

Two other doctors have also moved to the Sunshine Coast — one from Ohio and another from the U.K. — and a nurse practitioner will soon be arriving.

WATCH | 400 doctors, nurses have relocated from U.S. to B.C. in last year: 400 doctors, nurses have relocated from U.S. to B.C. in last year | Duration 2:05



Lyndsay Montina, the executive director of Sunshine Coast Division of Family Practice, said there has long been a doctor shortage in B.C.

"We've had some people that have been waiting for a family care provider for quite a long time, and so being able to have these new providers come, it's awesome," Montina said.

People who are looking for a family physician can visit the Health Connect registry.

World.title: 4 ex-Western University students accused in London, Ont., explosives-making scheme face 19 new charges
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The four people accused in a London, Ont., explosives and firearms-manufacturing investigation now face 19 new charges, according to court documents filed Tuesday.

Jerry Tong, Zekun (Alex) Wang, Fei (Frank) Han and Feiyang (Astrid) Ji were charged in January. All four were students or recent graduates of Western University, with the three men having studied in the engineering department.

The amended list of charges filed with the Ontario Court of Justice brings the total to 31 separate counts. Some of the charges are joint counts against all four, while others pertain to the specific accused.

The newest charges include possession of five specific explosive substances, possession of stolen property and access to computer data related to making firearms.

The lengthy investigation dates back to Jan. 24, when police responded to an overnight trespassing call at Western after two men entered one of the school's engineering buildings.

One person was arrested just outside the building. An investigation led police to a house in the nearby University Heights neighbourhood, where the other three were taken into custody.

Police spent days investigating inside the residence at 212 Chesham Place in London. (Alessio Donnini/CBC)

Police completed a multi-day search of the residence at 212 Chesham Place, where Wang, Han and Ji lived, as well as two additional homes in Orléans, in suburban Ottawa, and Gatineau, Que.

Firearms charges in other cities

When they were first arrested, the four faced multiple firearms charges, including the manufacturing of a handgun and possession of a loaded restricted handgun.

New charges against Tong, Wang and Ji include the possession of magazines and suppression devices, as well as possession of another prohibited firearm. Tong and Wang are also now accused of handing and carelessly storing a rifle.

Tong, who faces the majority of charges, also has new counts related to events in other cities. He's been charged with storing rifles at a home in Orleans, manufacturing a prohibited firearm in Ottawa and possessing a rifle at an unauthorized location in Quebec.

Court documents show that Tong held a firearms licence, but some of his charges relate to possessing a firearm at a place not indicated on his licence.

WATCH | How this Ontario home became the centre of a national security probe: How this Ontario home became the centre of a national security probe | Duration 2:14 Four people are in custody after police discovered chemicals they say could be used to create explosives at a home in London, Ont. But, new information shows the suspects were working on developing an anti-drone weapon system. Here’s what we know so far.

Tong and Wang also face new charges related to events that happened months before they were arrested.

Wang is now charged with manufacturing a weapon between Sept. 1, 2025, and Jan. 24, 2026, while the pair are charged with breaking into a Western building on Oct. 9, 2025.

Explosive substances revealed

Court documents also show that Tong, Wang, Han and Ji face a new list of charges for possessing explosive substances, and names them for the first time.

They are accused of possessing pentaerythritol tetranitrate (PETN), trinitrotoluene (TNT), dinitrophenol (DNP), hexamethylene triperoxide diamine (HMTD) and lead azide.

Originally, all four were charged with possession of precursor substances and finished high explosives.

London police are seen outside the home at 212 Chesham Place on Feb. 2. (Alessio Donnini/CBC)

All four also face a new count of possessing property of Western University valued at less than $5,000.

Wang faces a solo charge of accessing computer data that pertains to a firearm or a prohibited device, specifically, design files capable of being used with a 3D printer, metal milling machine or similar computer system for the purpose of manufacturing a device.

2 out on bail, 2 in custody

In total, these are the number of charges each accused faces:

Tong: 28.

Wang: 20.

Han: 11.

Ji: 13.

The four are still making their way through the courts, with two out on bail and two still in custody.

Tong did not request bail and remains in custody. Han was denied bail and remanded back into custody in February.

Wang was granted bail in March under strict conditions, including 24-hour house arrest and constant supervision from two sureties, who each posted $200,000. Ji is also out on bail with no sureties.

World.title: Hockey Canada suspensions remain for four 2018 world junior players acquitted in sex assault trial
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An independent appeal board has ruled that five players from Canada's 2018 world junior team acquitted last year of sexual assault breached the Hockey Canada code of conduct.

Hockey Canada said in a release Wednesday that it accepted the board's recommended continued suspensions and reinstatement dates for Alex Formenton, Cal Foote, Carter Hart, Dillon Dube and Michael McLeod.

The five were acquitted in July 2025 on sexual assault charges stemming from an encounter with a woman known as "E.M." at a 2018 Hockey Canada gala in London, Ont., celebrating the national junior team's world championship gold medal.

But the three-judge appeal board — John Laskin, Katherine Swinton and Thomas McEwen — recommended continued suspensions from Hockey Canada-sanctioned programs for four of the players.

McLeod will not be eligible for reinstatement until Nov. 10, 2030. Foote will be eligible on Nov. 10, while Hart and Dube will be eligible on that day in 2027 and 2028, respectively.

Formenton is eligible for immediate reinstatement.

Hockey Canada says all other players from the 2018 team are eligible for consideration to participate in any Hockey Canada-sanctioned program, effective immediately.

The suspended players, who all had NHL careers before the charges were filed, have been eligible to sign with NHL teams since Oct. 15 and able to play since Dec. 1.

Where are the five players now?

Hart signed with the Vegas Golden Knights and helped them reach this year's Stanley Cup final.

Dube became the second of the five to find NHL work when he signed with St. Louis on July 1.

McLeod played last season with Omsk Avangard of the Kontinental Hockey League,

Foote played last season with the American Hockey League's Chicago Wolves and recently had a one-year contract with Farjestad BK rescinded when the Swedish club received criticism for the signing.

Formenton has spent the last three seasons playing in Switzerland.

World.title: White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt to leave job at month's end, Trump says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt will leave her role at the end of the ‌month, U.S. President Donald Trump said Wednesday, leaving the president without one of his most trusted advisers ahead of November's midterm elections.

Leavitt will be an outside communications adviser and party operative shaping the future contours of Trump's "Make America Great Again" movement, she and Trump said in statements.

In a social media post, Leavitt, 28, said ​she aimed to spend more time with her young children. She gave ​birth to a daughter, her second child, in May and recently returned from maternity leave.

"Karoline has been a real leader in the White House, and has done a phenomenal job fighting for Justice, Liberty, and Freedom, ​since 2018, including our Historic Re-Election Campaign of 2024," Trump said in a social media post, ⁠calling Leavitt "one of the best ⁠White House Press Secretaries in the History of the Office."

Leavitt called ‌her role at the White House "the honor and adventure of a lifetime."

Leavitt joined Trump's 2024 ⁠campaign ⁠and ​served as transition spokesperson before Trump selected ​her to ⁠be White House press secretary. She was the youngest person to be appointed to the role.

Trump did not outline plans for who might replace her in the high-profile job.

Leavitt 'spoke Trump fluently'

"Few could or will ever compare to Karoline," said ⁠Harrison Fields, Trump's former principal deputy press secretary.

"She's someone who not only spoke Trump fluently, she knew how to feed the media beast in a cunning, audacious and successful way that, most importantly, played to her audience: the president."

Trump is seen speaking with reporters at Joint Base Andrews, in Maryland, on Tuesday, as Leavitt stands nearby. (Mark Schiefelbein/The Associated Press)

In her year and a half on the ‌job, Leavitt and White House communications director Steven Cheung transformed the administration's posture toward the media — in ways that some of Trump's allies cheered and free press advocates criticized.

The Trump administration began hand-picking which journalists receive access to the president, jettisoning the long-running system set up by the independent White House Correspondents' Association.

The press pool was traditionally a ​rotation chosen by the industry group to ensure media outlets had uniform access to the president and could relay his activities to the public and to other journalists who ⁠could not attend smaller gatherings.

As part of that process, the Trump administration press office created a special "new media" seat in the briefing ⁠room that gave podcasts, newsletters and fledgling digital outlets a more prominent role in covering the presidency.

Some press advocates hailed ⁠the move ⁠as a recognition of the changing media landscape. ​Others criticized it as a lever the administration could use to reward outlets whose coverage it saw as favourable.

World.title: Former Raptors coach fights Ontario over nearly $700K tax paid on multimillion-dollar home
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Former Toronto Raptors head coach Nick Nurse and his wife are embroiled in a legal dispute with the Ontario government over its refusal to reimburse the couple nearly $700,000 in foreign buyer tax they paid on their Mississauga home.

A notice of appeal dated July 6 and filed with the Ontario Superior Court of Justice alleges that the provincial government wrongfully denied Nurse and his wife a rebate for a non-resident speculation tax (NRST) they paid when they bought their home in 2021 for $4.65 million.

The provincial tax is applied to residential properties purchased by "individuals who are foreign nationals," according to the province's website.

The notice says Nurse and his wife Roberta "were not the type of real estate speculators the Legislature aimed to address."

The home was the principal residence for Nurse and his wife from 2021 to 2023, according to their appeal.

CBC News reached out to the Ministry of Finance for comment but has not yet received a response.

Nurse brought 'significant' value to province: appeal

The notice says that during the time Nurse lived at the property, he and his wife were foreign nationals in Canada. But it also says that Nurse held a foreign national work permit and was employed by Maple Leaf Sports and Entertainment LTD., the entertainment conglomerate that owns the Raptors, for nearly 10 years.

"Mr. Nurse brought significant economic and social value to the province," the notice of appeal said.

WATCH | How Nurse coached the Raptors to an NBA championship win: The rookie head coach that took the Toronto Raptors to an NBA Championship | Duration 2:06 Raptors head coach Nick Nurse has been an archetype of steady leadership, solid as a rock, and he has now taken the Toronto Raptors to the ultimate goal: an NBA Championship. But this didn't happen overnight for the Iowa native, he worked long and hard to get here.

Nurse led the Raptors to their first-ever championship win in 2019. He was fired in 2023 following a disappointing season when they did not make the playoffs, and then went on to coach the Philadelphia 76ers.

The notice of appeal says that in accordance with provincial rules, Nurse and his wife were eligible for an NRST rebate on the home.

In an email Tuesday, the lawyer representing the couple, Mike Collinge, said the law firm has "no further comment at this time."

According to the provincial government website, a foreign national can be eligible for an NRST rebate if specific conditions are met, which include:

Initially paying the NRST.

Becoming a permanent resident of Canada within four years from the date of purchase/acquisition of the property.

Occupying the property as their principal residence.

The government previously had transitional NRST rebates available, which granted foreign workers in Ontario the ability to get the rebate if they met specific criteria, so long as their agreement of purchase and sale was entered into on, or before, March 29, 2022. The application deadline for the rebate was March 31, 2025.

The notice of appeal states that Nurse and his wife applied for the rebate but it was rejected by the province because they did not occupy their home up to the date that they applied for the rebate.

The appeal alleges that was not a requirement at the time their rebate application was filed.

According to the court document, Nurse and his wife filed a rebate application in March 2024. They sold their Mississauga home in September 2023.

Their application was denied in April 2024, with Nurse and his wife filing a notice of objection challenging the decision. A back-and-forth of exchanges with the ministry ensued until the government confirmed its rejection on April 10 this year.

Nurse and his wife then filed their appeal. They are seeking a $697,500 rebate plus applicable interest and "further relief" as deemed appropriate by the court.
