World.title: US voters give both parties a reality check on their radical factions
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaUS election US voters give both parties a reality check on their radical factions Michael Koziol August 13, 2026 — 5:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It was always a bit unfair that US Democrats were put through the wringer over some of their more radical candidates for this year’s midterm elections, while Republicans escaped relatively unscathed. By and large, Republicans were not asked what it meant for their party that pillow mogul and famed election result denier Mike Lindell was seeking the Republican nomination to become governor of Minnesota – with President Donald Trump’s endorsement. My Pillow founder Mike Lindell failed to win the Republican primary in Minnesota as voters shied away from both parties’ extremes. AP Photo/Ellen Schmidt In part, that’s because election denial, conspiracy theories and the far-right are by now so entwined with the GOP that it has become a moot point. There is no question about a Trumpist takeover of the Republican Party – it has already happened. But there was a reality check on Tuesday night when Lindell, despite the president’s backing, lost the primary to Lisa Demuth, the speaker of the Minnesota House of Representatives.



It was a good evening for moderates in both parties – and a wake-up call, potentially, for their more extreme factions. In Wisconsin, state politician and declared democratic socialist Francesca Hong lost her bid to become the Democrats’ nominee for governor of Wisconsin, losing to establishment-backed candidate David Crowley in a tight contest that the polls got wrong. Francesca Hong narrowly lost to her establishment rival in the Democratic primary for governor of Wisconsin. AP Photo/Nam Y. Huh Hong, 37, came to national attention – and not in a good way – for some of her past statements, including a 2020 tweet arguing that Thanksgiving should be permanently cancelled because it celebrated colonialism. Asked on CNN whether she stood by that view, she told an anecdote about being a chef, in a widely circulated clip that some analysts believe cost her the win.



Hong tried and failed to win endorsements from progressive kingmakers Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who said they weren’t getting involved in gubernatorial races. View post on X But AOC was also critical of Hong’s excesses. “Woke 1 was crazy,” she said, laughing, on America’s ABC News on Sunday, attributing the phrase to one of her local councillors. She basically went on to say – in nicer language – that most people had moved on from some of the opinions they articulated during the COVID-19 pandemic, which more or less aligned with a time people now describe as “peak woke”. “Woke 1 was crazy”: Progressive hero Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said people had evolved from their COVID-era views. Bloomberg



“Especially during COVID, there was a huge opening of the Overton Window,” AOC said. “The doors were really opened in trying to entertain every and any policy that was going to get us to a better place.” She maintained that “the discussions that were had in that time were quite fruitful”. Abdul El-Sayed, the populist progressive Democrat who won a US Senate primary in Michigan last week – beating an establishment candidate backed by the party elite and $US60 million ($85 million) in outside funding – was a much different proposition to Hong. Related Article US politics Left-wing populist wins in Michigan as Democrats reject party establishment Articulate and seasoned, he had already recanted some of his earlier positions such as defunding the police – though he maintained a tough line on ending US military aid to Israel. In the end, voters were savvy enough to reward the reasonable candidate, and take a pass on the outlandish one who wasn’t sure about Thanksgiving and didn’t seem quite ready for prime time.



And in Minnesota, voters were smart enough to give Lindell a wide berth – not that he’ll admit it. The My Pillow founder refused to concede defeat on Tuesday night, insisting his team had found “anomalies” with the vote. My Pillow chief executive Mike Lindell and President Donald Trump at the White House in 2020. AP “I’m not going to sit by until these numbers are explained,” he said, to applause. “We will get a full report on this … I’ve been on the phone with a lot of people. As you know, I’m very good at looking at elections.” It was true to form. Lindell was one of the most vocal proponents of the false claim that the 2020 presidential election was stolen from Trump. He pushed false conspiracy theories about voting machines by the company then known as Dominion.

World.title: Millions ‘missing’ and no relief: Workers detail deepening crisis in Victoria’s mental health sector
World.content:
The crumbling state of Victoria’s mental health system has been exposed by workers who say they are being subjected to violence weekly and the sector is more broken now than it was before the royal commission. Their verdict comes as the government is asked to explain where $40 million to deliver 2000 homes for people with mental illness has gone and the fly-in, fly-out boss of the state’s flagship youth service quits. Professor Patrick McGorry is concerned about the lack of progress on mental health reform. Aaron Francis The Community Housing Industry Association [CHIA] Victoria has called on the Carroll government to come clean about its housing commitment, claiming it’s been quietly abandoned, and the funding has disappeared. The 2000 supported living places were a recommendation of the Royal Commission into Victoria’s Mental Health System and received $40.4 million in the 2021-22 budget, with pledges to provide the homes as part of the state’s Big Housing Build.



But progress on these spots has stalled, and the funding commitment has disappeared from future budget papers. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health FIFO boss leads Victoria’s flagship youth mental health service amid reports of patient deaths and violence CHIA chief executive Sarah Toohey said the government had so far broken its promise to deliver and fund the supported homes. “The government is quietly walking away from this royal commission recommendation to deliver mental health supported homes for Victorians,” she said. When asked about the project, the Carroll government pointed to 368 purpose-built mental-health supported dwellings constructed through the Social Housing Growth Fund, a program set-up in 2018.



Homes Victoria is also building 505 homes for people living with mental illness, but the CHIA says these are not yet “supported housing”, which requires funding for specialised staff and care. A government spokesperson did not detail what had happened to the money, but said they were delivering more homes for people with mental health challenges. “This is an important and complex reform, and we are taking a careful approach to ensure people living with mental health challenges get the long-term housing and specialist support they need.” More than five years after the royal commission handed down a final report, that then-premier Daniel Andrews promised to implement in full, an investigation by The Age has exposed serious failings in the sector and how it is being managed by government. This included that an independent watchdog’s report being reworked before its release so it was less critical of the government’s progress; a damning assessment on reform by advocate Patrick McGorry and accusations of violence, drug use and an exodus of senior staff from the state’s flagship youth mental health service.



Parkville Youth Mental Health and Wellbeing Service (PYMHWS) chief executive Dr Leanne Geppert on Wednesday resigned a day after The Age revealed she had been leading the organisation under a fly-in, fly-out arrangement. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health Kids’ mental health unit shut as staff investigated for use of force The service’s board chair, Cath Bowtell, announced Geppert was stepping down, thanking the Brisbane-based boss for her “extraordinary contribution”. “This has been a difficult and deeply considered decision for Leanne,” Bowtell said. “Having led PYMHWS through its establishment and first year of operations, she has been considering for some time when the right point would be to step away. Importantly to her, she wanted to see the organisation through a number of significant milestones.”



Frontline mental health workers across the state have also voiced their concerns at failed reforms promised by the royal commission. A survey of more than 500 workers across 11 Victorian health services reported a deterioration in conditions for patients and staff as well as escalating violence and drug usage in secure psychiatric wards. Two-thirds of mental health workers reported to the Health and Community Services Workers Union (HACSU) that they had been assaulted in the past year, with patients who are more acutely unwell on presentation contributing to the rise in aggression. “I have witnessed colleagues be punched so hard they are concussed, strangled, scratched, have blood-borne virus-infected blood spat at them, facial bones fractured,” one worker said. Another reported clients at their hospital were not being treated in appropriate timeframes, which meant their health deteriorated and the risk to staff increased.



“The consumers are not being actively treated and are being discharged too soon, often very unwell,” the mental health worker said. “Most recently a client [who] had an admission was discharged to [the] community and remained unwell. She was readmitted one week later and remains in the intensive care unit. She was not actively treated and now her in-admission is much longer than it should have been.” More than 48 per cent of survey respondents said they disagreed or strongly disagreed that their health services were better placed now than they were before the royal commission. Less than 15 per cent of the workforce said they believed the mental health system had improved, while the remaining workers were neutral in their opinions about the impact of the reforms.



“In so many ways we have gone backward since the royal commission and nothing has actually changed,” a worker wrote. “In fact, access to mental health care has been worse.” HACSU Victorian branch secretary Paul Healey said the survey responses painted a concerning picture of the reality facing mental health workers, consumers, carers and families across Victoria. ”We need to be clear that this is not about blaming people experiencing mental illness,” he said. “Mental health workers understand the complexity of mental health care and are committed to providing compassionate support. “But a system that is under-resourced, overstretched and unable to provide the right care at the right time, built on the broken promises of a royal commission, increases risks.



Related Article Opinion

Mental health I’m a psychiatrist of 40 years. It’s mass gaslighting to claim we’ve made progress Patrick McGorry Psychiatrist and mental health advocate “These workers have carried the system through enormous challenges. They deserve more than being told change is coming, change needs to happen now.” In parliament on Wednesday, Mental Health Minister Ingrid Stitt said her government was proud of the support they’d provided the mental health workforce. “We have increased the workforce by over 30 per cent in the mental health sector. We have increased the number of acute beds available across the system,” she said. “We have delivered modern fit-for-purpose services across the state, including at the Thomas Embling Hospital and including at youth recovery and prevention centres in every region in the state.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: A billionaire secretly anointed his youngest son as successor. His other children were blindsided
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two months before his death in Greece, billionaire Nick Andrianakos met his youngest son for lunch at upmarket Glen Iris restaurant Grazia, where he anointed him successor to the family’s petrol and property empire. The ailing founder of Milemaker Group told Theo Andrianakos he would have full control of the family’s multibillion-dollar businesses, and that his vast portfolio of assets in Australia and Greece would also be passed on to Theo and his two sons. Nick Andrianakos, pictured in Greece in 2022, aged 78. Athina Souli Theo also learned at the meeting in January 2025 that his father intended to bequeath €5 million ($8.17 million) to his substantially younger partner Hatouna Sakvarelintze, an architect the ailing businessman had met a couple of years earlier on a hotel redevelopment project. However, there was a sticking point in the patriarch’s grand succession plan – Andrianakos’ three other children, who would later claim in the Supreme Court of Victoria that the revised “family agreement” had not been relayed to them, nor formalised in a signed will. The death of the 81-year-old patriarch on March 17 last year – just days before he was due to sign the will and the family agreement – sparked a toxic legal battle between the siblings over control of their late father’s assets and extensive business interests. The case was set to proceed to trial last month, with siblings Kristina and Paul Andrianakos and Vicky Papamarkou relying on the original documents, signed by their father in 2018 and 2019, which gave the sisters a greater slice of their father’s $183 million estate, and the siblings shared control over Milemaker Group.



Under the signed will, Andrianakos wanted to give his sons the bulk of his inheritance – allocating them $83 million each, and his daughters $24 million respectively. However, the siblings reached an eleventh-hour agreement that avoided a trial and ultimately allowed Justice Peter Gray to grant probate of the unsigned will. Two city penthouses, listed as being worth more than $4 million, are among the division of assets. Domain The settlement, on July 17, handed Theo and his sons all of Andrianakos’ estate, which included CBD penthouses, beachfront homes on the Mornington Peninsula, and properties in Greece, along with a $200,000 black Bentley and a tractor. Theo received the lion’s share of the estate, reducing his brother’s inheritance and seeing his sisters receive substantially less than the $24 million they were originally entitled. The court dispute also laid bare the tensions between the family and Andrianakos senior’s partner, Sakvarelintze. The daughters claimed in respective affidavits that during the months that the drastic changes to their father’s estate were drafted, he had been frail and could no longer understand English.



Papamarkou warned her father that his Greek girlfriend was “probably only after his money” a year before he made changes to bequeath her millions, she claimed in her sworn statement. “I warned him that it was strange to see a woman so young be romantically interested in someone around 80 years of age,” she said in an affidavit. “I told my father to be careful because she was probably only after his money. My father responded by saying words to the following effect: ‘There is no way Hatouna is getting any of my money or property. I am leaving all my property to my children’.” The late billionaire’s wealth planner Peter Pagonis claimed the revised, unsigned will represented the lawful and legitimate plan for his inheritance. Pagonis, who consults to more than 450 ultra-high-net-worth families, said in an affidavit that the family patriarch first ordered him to draft the changes in November 2024 after expressing concerns the three siblings would seize control of Milemaker Group. Nick Andrianakos and son Theo. “The deceased said word to the effect that he was concerned that Vicky, Paul and Kristina would ‘gang up’ on Theo, who was CEO of Milemaker Group, and who was instrumental in operating and growing the Milemaker Group business with [Andrianakos],” he said.



“He was concerned his children Vicky, Paul and Kristina will disrupt the family legacy and seek to break up the family assets and the business that he had grown over time.” Pagonis said that Andrianakos told him in November 2024: “I want to make sure that Theo has full control of the business going forward.” The order came only a few months after the tense exchange between Papamarkou and her father over his romance, which had strained their relationship. She said after that confrontation in July 2023, the pair did not speak for some time until finally reconciling in August 2024. One of the family’s city penthouses. Domain Andrianakos’ instructions in November 2024 led to significant changes to the family agreement, the formal succession document which includes clauses of the family values (among them: family is first, business for future generations, integrity, and no drugs). The succession plans were later thrashed out over a series of meetings – including several lunches at Grazia and secret meetings at Andrianakos’ CBD penthouse – during what would be his last visit to Melbourne.



A $20,000 tractor was part of the estate. Kubpower.com.au The businessman jetted into town on Christmas Eve 2024 with Sakvarelintze, in time for the family’s Christmas lunch, held at Nobu in Crown Casino. Paul, Vicky and Kristina did not attend any of the estate discussions, with Papamarkou noting she didn’t discuss it with her father over Christmas lunch. “When the family met on Christmas day, my father appeared frail and unwell. Because the Christmas lunch was very busy, I did not get to spend any one-on-one time with my father that day,” she said. Papamarkou said when she did later catch up with her father, he was unwell and had difficulty getting up off the couch. Before returning to Greece in January 2025, Andrianakos visited Kristina’s home, where she claims he reassured her about his estate: “My father brought up his will again and told me that Vicky and I would be included and get a share of everything.” The Andrianakos family mansion sits on acreage in Greenvale. Justin McManus

World.title: ASX set to slide; ANZ posts $1.9b quarterly profit, home loan applications fall
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slide; ANZ posts $1.9b quarterly profit, home loan applications fall Stan Choe Updated August 13, 2026 — 8:11am ,first published 5:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wall Street edged near its record after several AI stocks reported better growth than analysts expected, while a report showed inflation across the United States was slightly less bad last month. The S&P 500 added 0.3 per cent and marked its first gain since setting its all-time high on Friday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped less than 0.1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 0.5 per cent. Stocks like Nvidia and Super Micro Computer helped lead the way on signals that businesses continue to spend big dollars on AI infrastructure. Treasury yields eased following the latest inflation data. Wall Street jumped as the AI trade reignited after some positive results while a report showed inflation across the United States dipped. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to fall, with futures at 5.54am AEST pointing to a fall of 19 points or 0.2 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.5 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.62¢. ANZ Bank says home loan applications have fallen 12 per cent since the May budget, excluding applications it received via a government deposit guarantee scheme, as it also reported $1.9 billion in cash profits for the latest quarter.



In a trading update for the June quarter, ANZ said its cash profits rose 1 per cent compared with the quarterly average for the March half. On Wall Street, stocks in the artificial-intelligence technology business helped lead the way after strong profit reports bolstered hopes they can continue to deliver big-enough growth to justify the huge gains their prices have made. Super Micro Computer, which sells servers and other equipment, jumped 19.6 per cent after reporting earnings per share for the latest quarter that were 84 per cent higher than analysts expected. It also gave forecasts for upcoming profit and revenue that topped analysts’ expectations. Related Article Opinion

Gold Gold is glittering again – but that’s not necessarily good news Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist CoreWeave, which offers AI computing power to customers over the cloud, leaped 19 per cent after reporting better revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, along with a milder loss. CEO Michael Intrator said demand is accelerating from customers as big businesses adopt AI.



CoreWeave gives its customers access to AI chips from Nvidia, and Nvidia climbed 3 per cent. It was the single strongest force lifting the S&P 500. It’s a return to strength for AI stocks, which have been veering on a roller-coaster ride. After surging to records, AI stocks came under pressure on worries that they shot too high. Investors wanted to see big spenders on AI prove that their investments are yielding enough in profits and productivity to make them worth it. That in turn could lead to continued demand for chips and other AI infrastructure. Wall Street also got some support from easing yields in the bond market. Treasury yields fell after a report showed that US consumers paid prices for gasoline, groceries and other costs of living last month that were 3.4 per cent higher than a year earlier. That’s higher than anyone would like, but it’s not as bad as June’s 3.5 per cent inflation rate. The deceleration could give the Federal Reserve more leeway to hold off on hikes to interest rates. Higher rates would help keep a lid on inflation, but it would do so by making it more expensive for US households and companies to borrow and forcing a slowdown in the economy. Higher interest rates also would undercut prices for stocks and other investments.



The Fed’s members have been notably split about whether they should have already begun hiking interest rates. But Wednesday’s update on inflation pushed traders to pull back on bets the Fed will hike its main interest rate at its next meeting in September. Traders are betting on just a 40 per cent chance of it, down from the coin flip’s chance seen the day before, according to data from CME Group. That helped pull the yield on the 10-year Treasury down to 4.68 per cent from 4.70 per cent late Tuesday. It, though, still remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran, which sent oil prices and worries about inflation spiking. Related Article Opinion

Property market Is it time to buy a house? Here is what the CBA chief would tell his kids Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Oil prices swung between modest gains and losses Wednesday, and the price for a barrel of Brent crude slipped 0.2 per cent to $US88.74.



Higher yields have already pulled long-term mortgage rates to their highest levels in a year. That’s hurting the housing industry, and losses for homebuilders on Wednesday helped keep the market in check. D.R. Horton fell 3.3 per cent, and PulteGroup lost 2.5 per cent. Builders FirstSource, which sells countertops and other building materials, dropped 1.9 per cent. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed across Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 3.7 per cent for one of the world’s bigger gains. It’s been at the center of the jarring swings for AI stocks because it’s dominated by two tech giants, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

ANZ Bank says home loan applications have fallen 12 per cent since the May budget, excluding applications it received via a government deposit guarantee scheme, as it also reported $1.9 billion in cash profits for the latest quarter.

In a trading update for the June quarter, ANZ said its cash profits rose 1 per cent compared with the quarterly average for the March half.

A key focus for investors is how the government’s move to rein in tax concessions for property investors is affecting mortgage lending, and rival banks have all revealed a significant drop in loan applications since the May budget.

Home loan applications for ANZ have fallen 12 per cent since the May budget. Will Willitts

ANZ reported applications were “broadly flat” in the June quarter compared with March, though this was supported by the bank joining the federal government’s 5 per cent deposit guarantee scheme from late March.

Joining the scheme meant the bank’s loan growth was stronger than it would have been otherwise.

Excluding the impact of the scheme, ANZ said the value of new mortgage applications fell 12 per cent in the period from the budget to late July, compared with the March quarter.

World.title: ‘Once in a lifetime’: Millions gather in Europe to see first total solar eclipse in decades
World.content:
WorldEuropeSpace ‘Once in a lifetime’: Millions gather in Europe to see first total solar eclipse in decades Corina Pons and Tom Little August 13, 2026 — 6:21am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Madrid/Reykjavik: The skies above Iceland fell into total darkness as a full solar eclipse occurred over the country’s westernmost coast, as a break in the clouds allowed holidaymakers and locals to glimpse the celestial phenomenon. Live footage from Reykjavik showed on Wednesday (Iceland time) that, despite the overcast sky, a cheer went up from the crowd gathered in front of Hallgrimskirkja church when everything went black above them. The total solar eclipse is seen in Palencia, Spain. Getty Images Millions of people gathered in Iceland and northern Spain to witness Western Europe’s first total solar eclipse in 27 years, with Spanish officials warning people to avoid areas where a heatwave has raised the risk of wildfires. Authorities were expecting up to 6 million visitors in mostly rural areas within the eclipse’s path across the north of Spain and the Balearic Islands, said Juan Cruz, Spain’s Secretary of State for Science.



“I hope that tonight will see the emergence of a wonderful generation of astrophysicists,” he said. “It’s such a special moment.” The eclipse was quickly followed by the sunset in Spain, making the event particularly alluring. The uncanny sensation when day briefly turns into twilight and some animals fall quiet as the moon passes directly between Earth and the sun, was often treated as an omen in the past, a cosmic struggle or a sign of divine power.



Now, Spain sees it as a chance to showcase seldom-visited regions and draw tourists away from its overcrowded beach resorts, while also rolling out a massive police operation and public safety campaign to prevent them from causing wildfires. Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska told reporters that 25,000 police officers had been assigned to guarantee security around the eclipse observation while nearly 100 planes and helicopters were also being deployed. People observing a partial eclipse at Northala Fields in London. AP Photo/Frank Augstein A man watches with a welding shield in Herten, Germany. AP Photo/Martin Meissner Lola Guerreiro spent the night in the mountains near Arcos de las Salinas in eastern Spain, home to Galactica – Europe’s largest educational astronomy centre – as well as the Javalambre observatory, after making the long drive from Extremadura to view the eclipse.



“Watching a total solar eclipse has been a dream of mine for many, many years, and I didn’t want to miss the chance to experience it, even though it meant a seven-hour journey,” she said. Sergio, a 60-year-old Italian, had made the trek in a camping van with his family to Arija in northern Spain. The eclipse seen at El Monte De San Pedro park in Spain. Getty Images People cast long shadows while watching from the top of a mine dump in Gremany. AP Photo/Martin Meissner “I do feel a little emotional. Yes, because I know I won’t have another chance in my life to see an eclipse, a phenomenon like this,” he said.



The Iberian Peninsula last saw a total solar eclipse in 1912. It is set to experience another one on August 2, 2027, and an annular eclipse in January 2028, completing the so-called “Iberian Eclipse Trio”. In Iceland’s capital Reykjavik, glasses to allow people to look at the phenomenon without damaging their eyes have been sold out for days as the Nordic country of roughly 400,000 people expects to welcome up to 80,000 visitors. The eclipse seen form Palencia, Spain. Millions gathered across the country to witness the event. Getty Images People observe the partial eclipse with special protective glasses in Liverpool, England. AP Photo/Jon Super Totality – when the moon completely covers the sun’s light – reached Iceland’s westernmost coast at about 5:44 pm local time (3.44am on Thursday, AEST). It cast the far west of the island nation into total darkness for more than two minutes, though most cities saw shorter periods of darkness. The moon’s shadow then continued its trajectory eastwards.



Authorities had warned of heavy traffic and urged viewers to arrive early. Singer Björk was due to perform a DJ set at an eclipse-themed event south of Reykjavik. US space agency NASA plans to fly a high-altitude WB-57 aircraft from Iceland to follow the moon’s shadow, and NASA-funded teams will launch balloons to study how the sudden darkness and cooling affect the lower atmosphere. A beachgoer wearing special eclipse glasses looks up from Puerto de Sagunto beach near Valencia, Spain. AP Photo/Alberto Saiz The moon and the sun set in the Gulf of Finland, seen from St. Petersburg, Russia. AP Photo/Dmitri Lovetsky Aside from casual observers, the event also draws “eclipse chasers”, enthusiasts who crisscross the globe to be in the path of totality whenever an eclipse occurs.



Gordon Telepun, a retired plastic surgeon and amateur astronomer from the U.S. who has photographed six total eclipses, said he would watch from the island of Mallorca because Spain checked all the boxes for eclipse chasers. World.title: LA Lakers sold in record $17.7b deal as Trump associate and former Disney chief swoop
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMergers & acquisitions LA Lakers sold in record $17.7b deal as Trump associate and former Disney chief swoop Randall Williams , Natasha Mascarenhas and Hannah Miller August 13, 2026 — 6:11am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Josh Kushner and Bob Iger are buying the Los Angeles Lakers basketball team for a record-breaking price of $US12.5 billion ($17.7 billion), according to people familiar with the matter. Kushner, managing partner and co-founder at Thrive Capital, and Iger, former chief executive officer of Walt Disney Co. who is also an adviser at Thrive, had been seeking to acquire an NBA expansion team in Las Vegas but pivoted to make an offer to buy the Lakers from financier Mark Walter, whose sprawling investment empire is under federal investigation. Joshua Kushner, with wife Karlie Kloss, is the younger brother of Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Bloomberg The first inquiry came from Iger-Kushner side and the deal moved quickly, with talks unfolding over a matter of three or four days and the final agreement coming together in the past 24 hours, Iger said in an interview with Bloomberg News on Wednesday. The deal represents a longtime dream of Iger, who has overseen billion-dollar NBA rights contracts for Disney’s ESPN division, but not owned a professional basketball team. It underscores the booming prices private equity firms are willing to pay for the top-tier sports franchises globally as those media rights continue to climb.



The executive recalled that Kushner, who is the brother of President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, likened buying the Lakers to purchasing the Mona Lisa. “This is a beachfront property on one of the best beaches in the world as I see it,” Iger said. Founded in 1947, the Los Angeles Lakers have been a powerhouse in the NBA. After moving from Minneapolis in 1960 to become the NBA’s first West Coast team, the Lakers have been in the finals 32 times and won 17 championships, establishing them as one of the most successful legacies in professional sports. Their “Showtime” era in the 1980s was led by superstar players like Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Magic Johnson. The fast-paced game the Lakers pioneered continues to influence the sport to this day. The Lakers are one of the most prestigious sports franchises in the world. AP The Lakers’ sale price is the highest ever for a US professional sports franchise, exceeding the $US9.6 billion paid for the National Football League’s Seattle Seahawks in July. “It’s stunning in terms of the amount and size,” said Lee Berke, CEO of sports media consultancy LHB Sports, Entertainment & Media. “If I was an NBA team, I’d be thrilled.”



Walter, who also owns the Los Angeles Dodgers baseball team and is an investor in English Premier League club Chelsea, bought a majority stake in the Lakers from the Buss family just over a year ago, in a deal valued at $US10 billion. Despite the change in majority owner, the league said at the time that Jeanie Buss, one of the children of the longtime owner Jerry Buss, would remain the team’s controlling governor for the foreseeable future. Former Disney chief Bob Iger. Bloomberg The billionaire CEO of Guggenheim Partners is dealing with a federal investigation into potential improprieties at two of his insurance companies and his global investment firm. Walter’s holding company, TWG Global, holds stakes in the sports teams as well as Walter’s insurance companies and in Guggenheim. Part of the inquiry involved representations Guggenheim made to outside parties about its revenue, Bloomberg reported in July. “Mark Walter and TWG have always acted in good faith, and those who have done business with Mark know him as honest and straightforward,” TWG Global, Walter’s holding company, said in a statement at the time. “We are cooperating with authorities, and we are confident these matters will be resolved favourably.”



Iger stepped down from the head of Disney, the parent company of ESPN, earlier this year but his association with sports goes back decades. A longtime Clippers fan, Iger previously worked at ABC Sports under media legend Roone Arledge and became the division’s vice president of programming in 1987. He joined Disney following the company’s acquisition of ABC and ESPN in 1996. The NBA aired on ABC from 1965 until 1973 and on ESPN between 1982 and 1984 before returning to both channels in 2002. Disney, Comcast Corp. and Amazon.com Inc. signed an 11-year, $US76 billion deal with the NBA in 2024 that kicked in with the league’s most recent season. Kushner and his newly formed holding company Thrive Eternal, which targets cultural institutions and sports franchises, made waves in the last two weeks when soccer’s governing body FIFA attempted to raise $US4.2 billion from investors including Thrive that would have created a for-profit arm housing the organisation’s media and commercial rights. The deal died after extreme pushback from UEFA and Concacaf. Mark Walter, pictured here with US President Donald Trump, bought a majority stake in the Lakers just over a year ago, in a deal valued at $US10 billion. Walter’s investment empire is under investigation. Getty Images One of Thrive Eternal’s first moves was buying a piece of the San Francisco Giants earlier this year, ploughing the money into the team’s stadium and surrounding real estate. Individually, Kushner had purchased stakes in the Memphis Grizzlies before selling that slice to acquire a piece of the Miami Heat. His aspirations to be the controlling owner of an NBA team went so far that he and Iger were interested in buying one of the potential NBA expansion teams in Las Vegas. As a result of the Lakers’ deal, Kushner will have to sell his piece of the Miami Heat. Karlie Kloss, Kushner’s wife, is a minority owner in WNBA team New York Liberty.



Related Article Opinion

FIFA World Cup How the Trump factor finally turned the soccer world against Infantino If Lakers fans are wondering what to make in the change of ownership, a trusted voice in the sport weighed in with his support: “Laker fans, you couldn’t have two better owners,” Johnson, a former part-owner of the team, said in a post on X. “I’ve known Bob personally for over 40 years — he has always loved the Lakers and basketball and he will bring championships back to LA.” Bloomberg The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: US voters give both parties a reality check on their radical factions
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaUS election US voters give both parties a reality check on their radical factions Michael Koziol August 13, 2026 — 5:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It was always a bit unfair that US Democrats were put through the wringer over some of their more radical candidates for this year’s midterm elections, while Republicans escaped relatively unscathed. By and large, Republicans were not asked what it meant for their party that pillow mogul and famed election result denier Mike Lindell was seeking the Republican nomination to become governor of Minnesota – with President Donald Trump’s endorsement. My Pillow founder Mike Lindell failed to win the Republican primary in Minnesota as voters shied away from both parties’ extremes. AP Photo/Ellen Schmidt In part, that’s because election denial, conspiracy theories and the far-right are by now so entwined with the GOP that it has become a moot point. There is no question about a Trumpist takeover of the Republican Party – it has already happened. But there was a reality check on Tuesday night when Lindell, despite the president’s backing, lost the primary to Lisa Demuth, the speaker of the Minnesota House of Representatives.



It was a good evening for moderates in both parties – and a wake-up call, potentially, for their more extreme factions. In Wisconsin, state politician and declared democratic socialist Francesca Hong lost her bid to become the Democrats’ nominee for governor of Wisconsin, losing to establishment-backed candidate David Crowley in a tight contest that the polls got wrong. Francesca Hong narrowly lost to her establishment rival in the Democratic primary for governor of Wisconsin. AP Photo/Nam Y. Huh Hong, 37, came to national attention – and not in a good way – for some of her past statements, including a 2020 tweet arguing that Thanksgiving should be permanently cancelled because it celebrated colonialism. Asked on CNN whether she stood by that view, she told an anecdote about being a chef, in a widely circulated clip that some analysts believe cost her the win.



Hong tried and failed to win endorsements from progressive kingmakers Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who said they weren’t getting involved in gubernatorial races. View post on X But AOC was also critical of Hong’s excesses. “Woke 1 was crazy,” she said, laughing, on America’s ABC News on Sunday, attributing the phrase to one of her local councillors. She basically went on to say – in nicer language – that most people had moved on from some of the opinions they articulated during the COVID-19 pandemic, which more or less aligned with a time people now describe as “peak woke”. “Woke 1 was crazy”: Progressive hero Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said people had evolved from their COVID-era views. Bloomberg



“Especially during COVID, there was a huge opening of the Overton Window,” AOC said. “The doors were really opened in trying to entertain every and any policy that was going to get us to a better place.” She maintained that “the discussions that were had in that time were quite fruitful”. Abdul El-Sayed, the populist progressive Democrat who won a US Senate primary in Michigan last week – beating an establishment candidate backed by the party elite and $US60 million ($85 million) in outside funding – was a much different proposition to Hong. Related Article US politics Left-wing populist wins in Michigan as Democrats reject party establishment Articulate and seasoned, he had already recanted some of his earlier positions such as defunding the police – though he maintained a tough line on ending US military aid to Israel. In the end, voters were savvy enough to reward the reasonable candidate, and take a pass on the outlandish one who wasn’t sure about Thanksgiving and didn’t seem quite ready for prime time.



And in Minnesota, voters were smart enough to give Lindell a wide berth – not that he’ll admit it. The My Pillow founder refused to concede defeat on Tuesday night, insisting his team had found “anomalies” with the vote. My Pillow chief executive Mike Lindell and President Donald Trump at the White House in 2020. AP “I’m not going to sit by until these numbers are explained,” he said, to applause. “We will get a full report on this … I’ve been on the phone with a lot of people. As you know, I’m very good at looking at elections.” It was true to form. Lindell was one of the most vocal proponents of the false claim that the 2020 presidential election was stolen from Trump. He pushed false conspiracy theories about voting machines by the company then known as Dominion.

World.title: Millions ‘missing’ and no relief: Workers detail deepening crisis in Victoria’s mental health sector
World.content:
The crumbling state of Victoria’s mental health system has been exposed by workers who say they are being subjected to violence weekly and the sector is more broken now than it was before the royal commission. Their verdict comes as the government is asked to explain where $40 million to deliver 2000 homes for people with mental illness has gone and the fly-in, fly-out boss of the state’s flagship youth service quits. Professor Patrick McGorry is concerned about the lack of progress on mental health reform. Aaron Francis The Community Housing Industry Association [CHIA] Victoria has called on the Carroll government to come clean about its housing commitment, claiming it’s been quietly abandoned, and the funding has disappeared. The 2000 supported living places were a recommendation of the Royal Commission into Victoria’s Mental Health System and received $40.4 million in the 2021-22 budget, with pledges to provide the homes as part of the state’s Big Housing Build.



But progress on these spots has stalled, and the funding commitment has disappeared from future budget papers. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health FIFO boss leads Victoria’s flagship youth mental health service amid reports of patient deaths and violence CHIA chief executive Sarah Toohey said the government had so far broken its promise to deliver and fund the supported homes. “The government is quietly walking away from this royal commission recommendation to deliver mental health supported homes for Victorians,” she said. When asked about the project, the Carroll government pointed to 368 purpose-built mental-health supported dwellings constructed through the Social Housing Growth Fund, a program set-up in 2018.



Homes Victoria is also building 505 homes for people living with mental illness, but the CHIA says these are not yet “supported housing”, which requires funding for specialised staff and care. A government spokesperson did not detail what had happened to the money, but said they were delivering more homes for people with mental health challenges. “This is an important and complex reform, and we are taking a careful approach to ensure people living with mental health challenges get the long-term housing and specialist support they need.” More than five years after the royal commission handed down a final report, that then-premier Daniel Andrews promised to implement in full, an investigation by The Age has exposed serious failings in the sector and how it is being managed by government. This included that an independent watchdog’s report being reworked before its release so it was less critical of the government’s progress; a damning assessment on reform by advocate Patrick McGorry and accusations of violence, drug use and an exodus of senior staff from the state’s flagship youth mental health service.



Parkville Youth Mental Health and Wellbeing Service (PYMHWS) chief executive Dr Leanne Geppert on Wednesday resigned a day after The Age revealed she had been leading the organisation under a fly-in, fly-out arrangement. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health Kids’ mental health unit shut as staff investigated for use of force The service’s board chair, Cath Bowtell, announced Geppert was stepping down, thanking the Brisbane-based boss for her “extraordinary contribution”. “This has been a difficult and deeply considered decision for Leanne,” Bowtell said. “Having led PYMHWS through its establishment and first year of operations, she has been considering for some time when the right point would be to step away. Importantly to her, she wanted to see the organisation through a number of significant milestones.”



Frontline mental health workers across the state have also voiced their concerns at failed reforms promised by the royal commission. A survey of more than 500 workers across 11 Victorian health services reported a deterioration in conditions for patients and staff as well as escalating violence and drug usage in secure psychiatric wards. Two-thirds of mental health workers reported to the Health and Community Services Workers Union (HACSU) that they had been assaulted in the past year, with patients who are more acutely unwell on presentation contributing to the rise in aggression. “I have witnessed colleagues be punched so hard they are concussed, strangled, scratched, have blood-borne virus-infected blood spat at them, facial bones fractured,” one worker said. Another reported clients at their hospital were not being treated in appropriate timeframes, which meant their health deteriorated and the risk to staff increased.



“The consumers are not being actively treated and are being discharged too soon, often very unwell,” the mental health worker said. “Most recently a client [who] had an admission was discharged to [the] community and remained unwell. She was readmitted one week later and remains in the intensive care unit. She was not actively treated and now her in-admission is much longer than it should have been.” More than 48 per cent of survey respondents said they disagreed or strongly disagreed that their health services were better placed now than they were before the royal commission. Less than 15 per cent of the workforce said they believed the mental health system had improved, while the remaining workers were neutral in their opinions about the impact of the reforms.



“In so many ways we have gone backward since the royal commission and nothing has actually changed,” a worker wrote. “In fact, access to mental health care has been worse.” HACSU Victorian branch secretary Paul Healey said the survey responses painted a concerning picture of the reality facing mental health workers, consumers, carers and families across Victoria. ”We need to be clear that this is not about blaming people experiencing mental illness,” he said. “Mental health workers understand the complexity of mental health care and are committed to providing compassionate support. “But a system that is under-resourced, overstretched and unable to provide the right care at the right time, built on the broken promises of a royal commission, increases risks.



Related Article Opinion

Mental health I’m a psychiatrist of 40 years. It’s mass gaslighting to claim we’ve made progress Patrick McGorry Psychiatrist and mental health advocate “These workers have carried the system through enormous challenges. They deserve more than being told change is coming, change needs to happen now.” In parliament on Wednesday, Mental Health Minister Ingrid Stitt said her government was proud of the support they’d provided the mental health workforce. “We have increased the workforce by over 30 per cent in the mental health sector. We have increased the number of acute beds available across the system,” she said. “We have delivered modern fit-for-purpose services across the state, including at the Thomas Embling Hospital and including at youth recovery and prevention centres in every region in the state.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: A billionaire secretly anointed his youngest son as successor. His other children were blindsided
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two months before his death in Greece, billionaire Nick Andrianakos met his youngest son for lunch at upmarket Glen Iris restaurant Grazia, where he anointed him successor to the family’s petrol and property empire. The ailing founder of Milemaker Group told Theo Andrianakos he would have full control of the family’s multibillion-dollar businesses, and that his vast portfolio of assets in Australia and Greece would also be passed on to Theo and his two sons. Nick Andrianakos, pictured in Greece in 2022, aged 78. Athina Souli Theo also learned at the meeting in January 2025 that his father intended to bequeath €5 million ($8.17 million) to his substantially younger partner Hatouna Sakvarelintze, an architect the ailing businessman had met a couple of years earlier on a hotel redevelopment project. However, there was a sticking point in the patriarch’s grand succession plan – Andrianakos’ three other children, who would later claim in the Supreme Court of Victoria that the revised “family agreement” had not been relayed to them, nor formalised in a signed will. The death of the 81-year-old patriarch on March 17 last year – just days before he was due to sign the will and the family agreement – sparked a toxic legal battle between the siblings over control of their late father’s assets and extensive business interests. The case was set to proceed to trial last month, with siblings Kristina and Paul Andrianakos and Vicky Papamarkou relying on the original documents, signed by their father in 2018 and 2019, which gave the sisters a greater slice of their father’s $183 million estate, and the siblings shared control over Milemaker Group.



Under the signed will, Andrianakos wanted to give his sons the bulk of his inheritance – allocating them $83 million each, and his daughters $24 million respectively. However, the siblings reached an eleventh-hour agreement that avoided a trial and ultimately allowed Justice Peter Gray to grant probate of the unsigned will. Two city penthouses, listed as being worth more than $4 million, are among the division of assets. Domain The settlement, on July 17, handed Theo and his sons all of Andrianakos’ estate, which included CBD penthouses, beachfront homes on the Mornington Peninsula, and properties in Greece, along with a $200,000 black Bentley and a tractor. Theo received the lion’s share of the estate, reducing his brother’s inheritance and seeing his sisters receive substantially less than the $24 million they were originally entitled. The court dispute also laid bare the tensions between the family and Andrianakos senior’s partner, Sakvarelintze. The daughters claimed in respective affidavits that during the months that the drastic changes to their father’s estate were drafted, he had been frail and could no longer understand English.



Papamarkou warned her father that his Greek girlfriend was “probably only after his money” a year before he made changes to bequeath her millions, she claimed in her sworn statement. “I warned him that it was strange to see a woman so young be romantically interested in someone around 80 years of age,” she said in an affidavit. “I told my father to be careful because she was probably only after his money. My father responded by saying words to the following effect: ‘There is no way Hatouna is getting any of my money or property. I am leaving all my property to my children’.” The late billionaire’s wealth planner Peter Pagonis claimed the revised, unsigned will represented the lawful and legitimate plan for his inheritance. Pagonis, who consults to more than 450 ultra-high-net-worth families, said in an affidavit that the family patriarch first ordered him to draft the changes in November 2024 after expressing concerns the three siblings would seize control of Milemaker Group. Nick Andrianakos and son Theo. “The deceased said word to the effect that he was concerned that Vicky, Paul and Kristina would ‘gang up’ on Theo, who was CEO of Milemaker Group, and who was instrumental in operating and growing the Milemaker Group business with [Andrianakos],” he said.



“He was concerned his children Vicky, Paul and Kristina will disrupt the family legacy and seek to break up the family assets and the business that he had grown over time.” Pagonis said that Andrianakos told him in November 2024: “I want to make sure that Theo has full control of the business going forward.” The order came only a few months after the tense exchange between Papamarkou and her father over his romance, which had strained their relationship. She said after that confrontation in July 2023, the pair did not speak for some time until finally reconciling in August 2024. One of the family’s city penthouses. Domain Andrianakos’ instructions in November 2024 led to significant changes to the family agreement, the formal succession document which includes clauses of the family values (among them: family is first, business for future generations, integrity, and no drugs). The succession plans were later thrashed out over a series of meetings – including several lunches at Grazia and secret meetings at Andrianakos’ CBD penthouse – during what would be his last visit to Melbourne.



A $20,000 tractor was part of the estate. Kubpower.com.au The businessman jetted into town on Christmas Eve 2024 with Sakvarelintze, in time for the family’s Christmas lunch, held at Nobu in Crown Casino. Paul, Vicky and Kristina did not attend any of the estate discussions, with Papamarkou noting she didn’t discuss it with her father over Christmas lunch. “When the family met on Christmas day, my father appeared frail and unwell. Because the Christmas lunch was very busy, I did not get to spend any one-on-one time with my father that day,” she said. Papamarkou said when she did later catch up with her father, he was unwell and had difficulty getting up off the couch. Before returning to Greece in January 2025, Andrianakos visited Kristina’s home, where she claims he reassured her about his estate: “My father brought up his will again and told me that Vicky and I would be included and get a share of everything.” The Andrianakos family mansion sits on acreage in Greenvale. Justin McManus

World.title: Housing plan stokes fears for 'taonga species' at Christchurch's Willowbank
World.content:
Christchurch Willowbank development worries wildlife reserve Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Christchurch's Willowbank Wildlife Reserve is sounding the alarm over a planned housing development next door, saying it could threaten the park's future.

The Christchurch City Council is consulting on a private plan change that would allow about 230 houses to be built on Willowbank's southern boundary.

The wildlife park and nature reserve has operated on the site for 52 years and is home to native wildlife including kea, tuatara, kākā, takahē, and kiwi.

DOC staff vaccinate a takahē at Willowbank Wildlife Reserve in Christchurch. Supplied / DOC

Willowbank director Mark Willis said noise, vibration, light pollution, and increased human activity from the development could disturb animals.

"We have both short-term and long-term concerns and think there needs to be more examination on what those impacts might be. The question really is, is it worth the risk for a few houses to jeopardise the unique work that an organisation like Willowbank does?," he said.

"We're highly involved with a number of what's known as New Zealand's taonga species and their conservation, and we know that these species are very sensitive to disturbance."

Willowbank directors and siblings Mark and Kirsty Willis. Supplied

Willis said Willowbank's kiwi breeding centre was situated not far from the boundary.

"We know kiwi by nature being nocturnal are sensitive to light, they have poor eyesight and they compensate by having exceptionally good hearing. They, through their feeding methods, are exceptionally sensitive to vibration," he said.

"They offer quite a good example as to why activities that would be generated by a large residential development might impact upon their wellbeing, their stress levels and ultimately whether they are going to breed."

The wildlife reserve has helped with the incubation and release of almost 700 kiwi into areas where they have been threatened, helping to stabilise their populations, he told Morning Report.

Kiwi had exceptional hearing and were very sensitive to noise, vibration and light, he said.

"We don't want to jeopardise the conservation work we do currently or what we might do in the future."

Willis was also concerned the reserve might end up having to restrict its operations if residents kicked up a fuss about noisy animals.

Supplied / Willowbank Wildlife Reserve

He said while it might sound fanciful to be a neighbour of a wildlife park, "the reality is our animals generate noise as loud as rock concerts - at any hour of the day or night. Animals and animal management also generate odours that residential neighbours may not enjoy."

"We are seriously concerned that complaints from new neighbours will lead to constraints on Willowbank's operations that limit our conservation efforts, animal wellbeing, and our ability to continue as a much-loved community experience as it is for so many today.

"Not only is our current boundary close to our existing activities but it is the obvious area should we need to expand those activities which would just bring them closer and closer to that residential activity and make the effect of it more and more pronounced."

Willis acknowledged some mitigation measures had been proposed in the plan change - including the requirement for housing next to Willowbank to have ventilation systems so people did not need to open windows -but he believed the reserve needed to be protected by a special purpose zoning.

The submission period for the plan change closes on 21 August.

World.title: Police manager sorry for 'confusion' over Superintendent Rakesh Naidoo's bid to stand for Labour
World.content:
Superintendent Rakesh Naidoo's manager has apologised for not informing the commissioner of police that Naidoo was considering standing for the Labour Party until a week after their initial conversation.

Assistant Commissioner Tim Anderson apologised to both Police Commissioner Richard Chambers and Naidoo for "the confusion, which has resulted in incorrect information being provided to media".

It comes after RNZ revealed on Wednesday Naidoo told Anderson he was considering standing as a candidate for the Labour Party about two weeks before he was confirmed as a list-only candidate.

Naidoo was confirmed on 8 June as a list-only candidate for Labour, and his ranking at 13th meant he was almost guaranteed a seat in Parliament.

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

He was an ethnic, iwi and communities relationships manager for police.

Chambers earlier said his role in the police was now untenable, and he should have told him earlier of his political intentions.

Assistant Commissioner Tim Anderson. RNZ / Nick Monro

The police manual said someone of Naidoo's rank had to inform the commissioner of that.

A review was underway into the period during which Naidoo was engaging with the Labour Party.

RNZ requested under the Official Information Act (OIA) all correspondence between Naidoo and Chambers and anyone else in police regarding his intention and subsequent decision to stand for Labour. RNZ also requested all correspondence between Naidoo and anyone associated with the Labour Party since January.

On Wednesday, police supplied RNZ with the requested information.

Chief assurance officer Mike Webb said there was no correspondence between Naidoo and Chambers.

The first conversation between Naidoo and his manager Anderson about the matter took place in the week commencing 25 May.

"Superintendent Naidoo verbally advised AC Anderson he was considering standing as a candidate for the New Zealand Labour Party, although, at that stage, he had not decided to do so.

"On Thursday 28 May, Superintendent Naidoo provided AC Anderson with printed copies of police policies, guidelines from the Public Service Commission and extracts from the Electoral Act 1993 which were relevant to steps that may need to be taken if he decided to stand for elected office."

In a statement to RNZ on Thursday, Anderson confirmed Naidoo spoke to him a week prior to his notification to the commissioner, advising that he had been approached to stand as a candidate in the general election.

"At the time Superintendent Naidoo had not reached a decision on whether to stand and I therefore treated our conversation as a confidential discussion and did not inform the commissioner of this conversation.

"When Superintendent Naidoo spoke to me again the next week to advise that he would be putting his name forward for a list ranking process, I immediately notified the commissioner of Superintendent Naidoo's intent."

Anderson said that "in hindsight, it would have been helpful for me to have advised the commissioner of Superintendent Naidoo's first approach.

"I have apologised to both Superintendent Naidoo and Commissioner Chambers for the confusion, which has resulted in incorrect information being provided to media."

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said he welcomed the apology and the "correction of the information provided to media at the time".

"As I have previously said, Rakesh Naidoo is a man of the utmost integrity, and I am confident he has conducted himself respectfully and followed appropriate processes."

The documents released under the OIA revealed that in the early afternoon of 4 June, Naidoo told Anderson in person that he was putting his name forward for the Labour Party's list, and confirmed that he would be attending a Labour Party moderating meeting on 6 June.

"Assistant Commissioner Anderson verbally briefed this information up to Commissioner Chambers by telephone at 3:21pm the same day.

"In a further verbal communication after his call to the Commissioner, AC Anderson spoke again briefly with Superintendent Naidoo."

Naidoo next contacted Anderson at about 1.20pm on 7 June, informing him he had been selected for a place on the Labour Party's list, and would make a decision on whether he would accept it that day.

Anderson then updated Chambers.

Richard Chambers. Calvin Samuel / RNZ

About 5.30pm, Naidoo met in person with Anderson and confirmed he would accept the list placement. He then sent an email to Anderson titled "New Zealand General Election 2026".

In the email, Naidoo said he was standing for the Labour Party as a list candidate and that his candidacy would be announced the following day.

"I intend to continue my service in police, in an apolitical manner until 30 September 2026. I will follow and respect the police, electoral and public service guidelines during this period."

On 30 September he would take leave, before nomination day, which is 8 October.

"On election day 7 November 2026 I will have an indication whether I have been successful in the 2026 General Election."

If he was successful, Naidoo would "officially retire/resign" on 27 November, the date the official results are announced.

"If I have not been successful, I will resume my duties on the first working day after polling day or at a mutually agreed time with Police."

Webb told RNZ that following checks of Naidoo's email account there were no messages directly received or sent from or to an @labour.co.nz address from January until 10 June.

"Superintendent Naidoo was the recipient of a small number of emails primarily relating to community events or engagements, of which an email address with a @labour.org.nz domain was also a recipient; one of which Superintendent Naidoo sent a 'reply all' message to that email.

"However, it is clear from the exchange that it does not bear upon Superintendent Naidoo's plans or subsequent decision to offer himself for elected office."

Parallel checks of Naidoo's police email traffic were also completed to check for any exchanges with any of the 34 current Labour Party members of parliament.

"A total of 239 emails were found to have been sent to or from @parliament.govt.nz addresses, only three of which were sent by Superintendent Naidoo.

"None of the identified emails to or from an @parliament.govt.nz address were found to raise concern, or bear upon Superintendent Naidoo's plans or subsequent decision to offer himself for elected office. Rather, all correspondence appeared to relate to the Superintendent's role as National Ethnic Partnerships Manager for Police, many relating to his work with ethnic communities."

The review

Chambers earlier said a review will be undertaken over the period during which Naidoo was engaging with the Labour Party, prior to him advising NZ police of his candidacy intentions.

"That review will include meetings he was involved in as a senior Police leader, the information he was privy to by virtue of his position, and whether anything was shared with any third party that should not have been shared.

"As a senior police officer, Superintendent Naidoo was privy to sensitive information and I need to be reassured information he has been privy to through the course of his duties has been handled properly.

"If anything of concern comes out of that, it will be assessed against the Police Code of Conduct."

Hipkins earlier told Morning Report Naidoo had followed process by informing his manager.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins. Zach Cornelisen / RNZ

"I think when you tell your boss, and your boss says, 'Okay, I'll pass that on to the commissioner,' I think you can assume that that means that you've done your duty of making sure the commissioner's been informed."

He said Labour had been speaking with Naidoo for a couple of months, and had agreed to a shortened selection process for him if he chose to stand.

"He wouldn't have to confirm with us until quite late in the piece that he was intending to proceed with a candidacy because he was very conscious, and we were very conscious, that the political neutrality of the police is incredibly important - and I think he's acted with the utmost integrity here."

Police Minister Mark Mitchell earlier said Naidoo had been privy to sensitive information.

World.title: National’s Asian candidates face uphill battle to secure seat in Parliament
World.content:
Eleven candidates of Asian heritage were included on National's party list that was unveiled on Saturday.

Incumbent MP Nancy Lu is the highest-ranked Asian candidate on the list, sitting in 16th place and improving on the 20th position she received in the 2023 rankings.

Meanwhile, an unprecedented eight candidates on the list are of Indian descent.

However, all National candidates of Asian descent face an uphill battle to get into Parliament based on current polling.

The latest 1News Verian poll unveiled Wednesday gives Labour top spot with 30 percent of the party vote, followed by National at 29 percent, the Green Party at 12 percent, ACT at 9 percent, New Zealand First and the Opportunity Party both at 8 percent, and Te Pāti Māori at 1 percent.

This result would give the ruling coalition 57 seats in total, with National picking up 36, ACT 11 and New Zealand First 10.

On the other side of aisle, Labour would get 38 seats, the Greens 15 and Te Pāti Māori six. Their total would be 59.

The Opportunity Party could enter Parliament for the first time with nine seats.

Lu, who is once again standing as a list-only candidate for National in this year's ballot, will be hoping to know her fate on election night - unlike what happened in 2023.

Lu failed to secure a seat in Parliament on 14 October last election when preliminary election results were declared.

However, when Andrew Bayly - then a National list MP - won a by-election in Port Waikato in November 2023, it propelled Lu into the Beehive as the next candidate on the party list.

Carlos Cheung, another incumbent MP of Chinese heritage, looks like he needs to defeat Labour's Michael Wood again to win the Mt Roskill electorate if he wishes to return to office.

Melissa Lee, a senior MP of South Korean heritage who has been in Parliament since 2008, has been ranked 30th on National's party list.

The six-term lawmaker and former broadcasting minister was ranked 13th in 2023.

After sitting on the back benches as an MP for five terms, Lee was given the ethnic communities, economic development, and media and communications portfolios following the coalition government's election victory in 2023.

In April 2024, Prime Minister Christopher Luxon dumped Lee from Cabinet and stripped her of the media and communications portfolio.

Lee lost her remaining ministerial roles in January 2025.

However, Luxon on Saturday backed Lee to win Mt Albert from Labour's Helen White, who won the electorate in 2023 by just 18 votes.

Mt Albert is historically a Labour stronghold, with former Prime Ministers Helen Clark and Jacinda Ardern representing it in Parliament.

The electorate has voted left ever since its inception in 1946.

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong is also contesting the Mt Albert seat, which makes the electorate one of the most interesting to watch in November.

National has eight candidates of Indian heritage on its party list, three more than it did in 2023.

Mahesh Muralidhar, the highest-ranked Indian-origin candidate on the list, jumped 19 places to 24th place this year.

However, it looks like Muralidhar needs to win the Tāmaki electorate to enter Parliament.

Muralidhar lost to Green Party leader Chlöe Swarbrick in Auckland Central by less than 4000 votes in 2023.

This year, he has switched to Tāmaki, which has been a National stronghold for decades before former ACT deputy leader Brooke van Velden turned it pink in 2023.

Luxon on Saturday expressed confidence Muralidhar would win Tāmaki in November.

"I am very confident about that," Luxon said.

Other five candidates of Indian heritage fighting for electorate seats on the list are Ankit Bansal in Palmerston North (list ranking 53), Lalit Arya in Ōtāhuhu (list ranking 59), Sunil Kumar in Glendene (list ranking 63), Karuna Muthu in Wellington Bays (list ranking 64) and Ghouse Majeed in Manurewa (list ranking 66).

The remaining two list-only candidates of Indian descent are Robin Atwall and Ash Nayyar, who sit near-bottom at 70 and 71 respectively.

Such low rankings give them little chance of securing a seat in Parliament unless there's a major upset on election night.

Aside from Tāmaki, the five electorates in which Indian-origin candidates are standing are opposition strongholds.

Luxon, however, is betting on Bansal to win Palmerston North in November.

When asked on Saturday about National not having any Kiwi-Indian representation in the Parliament for some time, Luxon praised returning candidate Bansal for doing "an exceptionally good job over the last three years".

"[Bansal] got the party vote win there [Palmerston North]," Luxon said.

"He obviously stayed very connected to the community, very engaged, very passionate about Palmerston North, and I think he's got a good chance there as well."

Bansal ran on the National ticket for the first time in 2023 against Labour MP Tangi Utikere, managing to secure 12,195 party votes to Labour's 11,293.

World.title: Wellington's after-hours clinic doesn't have staff to extend hours
World.content:
Wellington's after-hours medical service (WAMC) says it doesn't have the staff to extend opening hours to help it cope with a winter surge of patients.

Wellington Hopsital's emergency department had one of its busiest days in almost a year on Monday, seeing 258 patients,

Health NZ said the GP-run urgent care clinic would be extending its hours in an effort to cope with the influx. It was aiming to do this within six months of signing a contract.

But the clinic said it was still in negotiations with the agency and hadn't yet reached an agreement.

It said a new workforce model would have to be agreed before the hours could be extended and the change could take up to 15 months.

It said it was in contract discussions about funding and staffing.

World.title: Concerns potential buyers of Kāinga Ora house not told of 'meth lab' history
World.content:
Lower Hutt residents concerned property history kept hidden Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Neighbours who say they were terrorised by the former occupants of a Kāinga Ora house fear prospective buyers haven't been told about the home's history as a "meth lab".

The deadline sale for the two-bedroom Kāinga Ora property in the Lower Hutt suburb of Naenae closed on Tuesday, but Langford Street's residents say its chequered past hasn't been disclosed.

The 1940s home was billed as a "project you don't want to miss" and being offered for sale on an "as-is, where-is basis".

On Monday, a post-it note was plastered on the 'for sale' sign on the property's front lawn and across half a dozen of the home's windows and doors: "Warning. This house was previously a meth lab for years. Buyer beware."

Neighbours say crews arrived in "hazmat suits" a year ago to strip and clean the property, with Kāinga Ora confirming the home has undergone remediation for methamphetamine contamination.

Regional director for Greater Wellington Sarah Willson said the relevant reports were given to the listing agent, but a neighbour said they've received no toxicology reports despite multiple requests.

Bayleys residential sales manager Bhakti Mistry declined to comment.

'A terrifying time'

The Kāinga Ora house was the target of a drive-by shooting and multiple police raids, according to neighbours, before it was vacated about 18 months ago.

For a period of a couple of years, they said people would come and go from the home at all hours of the day and night and described drug deals, fights, and a rotating cast of gang members at the property.

Kāinga Ora said it couldn't comment on previous tenancies due to privacy considerations.

Barry - a resident on the street for 30 years - said it was a "terrible" and "frightening" time, with the occupants making no effort to hide what was going on.

"I see cars pull up. They'd ... tap on the window. People would pass out the drugs ... and they would drive off. This would happen continuously, a dozen times a day," he said.

"It's hard to describe just how bad it was. It was not just a simple drug-dealing house. It was a place where everyone hung out and parked on the berms ... just total chaos."

Police outside the property in July 2023. Supplied

The problematic behaviour culminated in a drive-by shooting one night, he said, describing the noise of the gun as "incredible," and showing RNZ what he claimed were multiple bullet holes in the Kāinga Ora home.

He said the spray of bullets also caught the house next-door.

Another neighbour, Benjamin said he remembered picking up casings in the aftermath and maintained it was luck no-one was hit.

"Honestly, it was a terrifying time. We didn't know what was going to happen next. We didn't know whether there was going to be an all out gun fight on the front lawn across the street and our kids would be collateral damage.

"We didn't know if the next drive-by they'd just shoot in our direction."

Damage following what residents describe as a drive-by shooting. Supplied

Three of the street's residents said crews in head-to-toe protective gear arrived to strip and clean the home once it was empty, with Benjamin saying they were at pains to protect themselves.

"They're putting on their hazmat suits and getting fully kitted-up."

Barry said the cleaners were at the property "on and off" for about two months, scrubbing walls and removing gib.

"I spoke to [one of the cleaners] and he said it's really bad, one of the worst he's seen.

"Whatever drugs they were cooking up ... [it's] penetrated throughout the whole house."

The property is to be sold 'as is, where is' after remediation for methamphetamine. RNZ

Meth remediation completed - Kāinga Ora

The neighbours told RNZ they were concerned that prospective buyers could be in the dark about the home's history.

Benjamin said it's been close to two weeks since he requested to see reports about methamphetamine contamination and remediation, but they have not been provided.

In a text exchange seen by RNZ, the agent said they did not have a toxicology report, but had requested it.

Bayleys declined to comment, directing RNZ to Kāinga Ora.

Willson said following the previous tenancy ending, the property was tested for methamphetamine contamination and specialist contractors completed remediation work.

"We advised the listing agent that the property had undergone methamphetamine remediation and have provided the relevant remediation reports to support the sale process."

Kāinga Ora declined to answer RNZ's follow-up question about when those reports were provided.

Langford Street RNZ

Director at law firm Pidgeon and Judd, Joanna Pidgeon said years ago there had been "massive issues" with methamphetamine contamination, with companies testing for meth also providing remediation service, giving them a "nice little income stream".

She said legislation fixed that issue and in 2018, former chief science advisor Sir Peter Gluckman established guidelines for acceptable levels of meth contamination in the home - below 15μg per 100cm2 where the drug had been smoked, and below 1.5μg per 100cm2 for manufacturing.

Pidgeon said if a meth-contaminated home had been remediated to below those levels, there was no obligation for the listing agent to disclose it to prospective buyers - unless specifically asked.

"Then they have to tell you the answer."

She said if the vendor had a report but didn't provide it, they would be implicated in the non-disclosure.

Pidgeon said information about contamination could affect whether someone was willing to buy the property and for what price, and said for one of her clients it was a deal-breaker.

"They just couldn't bear the thought of their baby...crawling around on floor that may or may not have some contamination. It wasn't something that they were prepared to deal with, but their agreement was conditional on it, so they were able to exit on that basis."
