Pidgeon said if purchasers learned of contamination after signing an agreement, exiting it or negotiating the price was possible, but would depend on factors such as the level of contamination and context around whether it should have been disclosed.

Bad reputation

Langford Street in Naenae. RNZ

Benjamin stressed he had no idea how contaminated the house was or still is, but said that was the problem. Someone trying to do their due diligence could be just as clueless as him, he said.

"They may have done an excellent remediation job and it's completely removed all contamination - and that would be amazing. It's just that we don't have that information."

Barry said regardless of the contamination, he didn't think the home was fit-for-purpose and wanted to see it bowled.

"It's got that bad a reputation. I wouldn't want to see a family in it with people still wanting to turn up and thinking it's a viable drug house.

World.title: 'Huge demand on services': North Shore ambulance patients diverted to Whāngarei
World.content:
Wellsford GP on Auckland ambulance patients sent to Whangarei Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Some Auckland ambulance patients are being taken to Whāngarei Hospital because North Shore Hospital is too full to take them.

That is despite the much smaller Whāngarei Hospital already struggling with extremely high patient numbers this winter.

RNZ understands diversions were taking place on Tuesday night which was also very busy at Whāngarei's emergency department.

Diversions were happening also last week.

Tim Malloy is a GP for Coast to Coast healthcare group which has a clinic in Auckland's most northern town Wellsford, just shy of the Northland border.

He was sent a letter by St John Ambulance last week telling him any patients from the northern part of the Rodney district who needed to go to an ED would be taken to Whāngarei. They were normally serviced by North Shore.

That was "due to the huge demand on the services at North Shore Hospital", he said.

RNZ understands Whāngarei was already under serious pressure itself. It is about half the size of North Shore.

Health NZ director of operations Brad Healy said it was a "very small number" of ambulances that were actually diverted to Whangarei.

"This practice is not unusual and used at times to manage demand and ensure patients can receive care as quickly as possible. In some instances, depending on the location of the patient, Whangārei Hospital is closer in travel time than North Shore Hospital," he said.

Malloy said the letter was the first his practice had ever received about the ambulance diversions.

Busy winter in northern Auckland

This winter was the busiest Malloy had seen in 37 years as a GP.

Patients in Coast to Coast's urgent care clinic were sometimes waiting five hours and staff have had to be brought in on their days off to help, he said

"When you have 15 people waiting for you and you have a serious illness you are trying to manage in a patient while you wait for an ambulance to arrive, and all these patients are just having to wait, it's incredibly stressful. For all of us," he said.

Most of the patients coming into urgent care had respiratory infections. The cases seemed to last longer - and there were a growing number of secondary infections, he said.

There were very high numbers of people with influenza and it was "hammering all our communities".

It was proving to be a particularly severe winter with patients sicker for longer and illnesses were affecting not just the vulnerable but also normally healthy people.

He told Morning Report patients were grateful to get any help so it was "slightly academic" to them whether their ambulance headed north or south.

Malloy wanted to see a campaign to encourage people to get vaccinated against flu - and for those vaccinations to be free.

It would help people stay healthy, in particular to avoid serious complications.

That would help the whole health system, he said.

World.title: Former Gloriavale members seek damages after Employment Court win against Labour Inspectorate
World.content:
Nine former Gloriavale members are seeking damages and declarations of slavery and servitude following a court ruling that the Labour Inspectorate made legal errors in two employment investigations.

Hosea Courage, Daniel Pilgrim, Levi Courage, Serenity Pilgrim, Anna Courage, Rose Standtrue, Crystal Loyal, Pearl Valor and Virginia Courage claimed they were failed by labour inspectors who did not properly investigate extremely serious allegations of forced labour, child labour, slavery and servitude at the Christian community in 2017 and 2021.

Their application for judicial review has succeeded in the Employment Court, after chief judge Christina Inglis found the Labour Inspectorate misunderstood its jurisdiction and failed to consider children.

"This case involved very high stakes, namely concerns about child and forced labour in a closed community with an Old Testament ethos," she said.

"The Labour Inspector was well aware that children were working within Gloriavale and were a significant category of vulnerable individuals who were effectively removed from the scope of the investigation without good reason."

The court earlier found the three men and six women were Gloriavale employees, rather than volunteers, in two landmark rulings in 2022 and 2023.

At an Employment Court hearing in March, the leavers challenged the lawfulness of the inspectorate's decisions in 2017 and 2021 not to fully investigate or take enforcement action as a result of allegations of employment law breaches, including child labour, forced labour and excessive working hours at Gloriavale.

They worked at the community from a young age, some in Gloriavale's commercial enterprises such as moss and rendering factories and honey and dairy businesses, and others in commercial-sized kitchens and laundries.

In 2017 Charities Services referred concerns about child labour, long hours and health and safety at Gloriavale's businesses to the Labour Inspectorate.

The inspectorate conducted a "desktop inquiry", with the report noting that if Gloriavale members were considered employees "there would inevitably be many serious breaches of employment law".

The report instead concluded that "on balance" people working at Gloriavale were likely "partners" or "volunteers" rather than employees, therefore it lacked jurisdiction to investigate further and closed the file.

Following media reports of poor working conditions and long work hours three years' later, two labour inspectors and four WorkSafe inspectors visited Gloriavale in September 2020.

Before a second visit in February 2021, the inspectorate decided to exclude children from the investigation.

Crown lawyers told the Employment Court the decision not to interview children was because they would need parental consent, the process would likely be intimidating or confusing and it was a better use of resources to confine the investigation to partners in Gloriavale's businesses and women working on the domestic teams.

The inspectors interviewed 39 current and 13 former members.

The 2021 report concluded that "members of the Gloriavale community cannot currently be considered to be employees and that the Labour Inspectorate therefore has no jurisdiction to investigate further".

The Employment Court found the Labour Inspectorate misunderstood its jurisdiction because inspectors wrongly believed they had to be satisfied that workers were "employees" before taking steps to investigate.

The court noted that an inspector's investigative powers were activated when they had "reasonable cause to believe" an employment relationship existed, not when it was proven on the balance of probabilities.

A person's employment status was a matter for the Employment Relations Authority or the court, Inglis said.

"It would put the cart before the horse to conclude that there was no employment relationship and so no power to investigate employment status," she said.

The court also found that the Labour Inspectorate's failure to investigate the position of Gloriavale children in 2017 and 2021 was an error of law, with legislation defining an "employee" as a person of any age.

Given the inspectorate was explicitly warned by Charities Services about work children were doing, including that 14 and 15-year-olds were working in commercial dairies and butchering, the position of children was a mandatory consideration, the court said.

"I have no difficulty concluding that the position of children known to be working in Gloriavale was such a plainly relevant factor that the Labour Inspector was required to consider it," Inglis said.

"Allegations of child labour had been made with profound implications for those impacted. The stakes were very high and called for a protective, rather than hands-off approach by the statutory officer charged with an investigative and enforcement function.

"Ignoring the position of child workers, without inquiry, was not a reasonably available option given the context within which the Labour Inspector was exercising their powers."

The inspectorate also knew that the number of children at Gloriavale significantly outweighed the number of adults and that the community was running multiple businesses and operations relying entirely on its own resources.

Excluding children from the investigation to save resources or avoid consent issues was irrational, the judgment said.

The 2021 report included advice from Crown Law that some community members were in a "grey area" because they had not signed Gloriavale's partnership agreement.

The court found it was unreasonable for the labour inspectors to accept signed partnership agreements at face value while ignoring other crucial documents they possessed, such as Gloriavale's foundational document What We Believe.

"The documentation, including What We Believe, was a large red flag as to the pervading features of the community, including the leadership's approach to work; the controlled environment in which residents lived; and the way in which external agencies were to be engaged with," Inglis said.

"Loud alarm bells ought to have been ringing from even a cursory reading of What We Believe, because the documentation makes it clear where the true power lay."

The document established that the community's leadership held absolute power over workers, dictated that members could not report concerns to external agencies and threatened eternal damnation for disobedience.

The court found that ignoring these clear indicators of duress and control was inexplicable, unreasonable and irrational.

The investigative process was also flawed because inspectors failed to allow the interviewed leavers to comment on the counter-narrative provided by Gloriavale's leadership, the court said.

By closing the inquiry without taking that step, the labour inspectors failed in their duty to adequately inform themselves.

Given the adverse findings and the vulnerability of those affected, the court suggested referring a copy of the judgment to the Attorney-General, Workplace Relations and Safety Minister and the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment chief executive.

World.title: Bridges not up to scratch, roads to be returned to gravel - South Island counts cost of under investment
World.content:
South Island leaders call for fairer funding for roads Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Only one in $9 of government roading funds gets spent in the South Island, a new report obtained by RNZ reveals.

The south accounts for almost a quarter of the country's population, 22 percent of GDP, a third of export goods and 40 percent of international visitor spending, but receives only 11 percent of transport spending.

Local political and business leaders say the lack of investment is disappointing.

Southland mayor Rob Scott has told RNZ that trucks are unnecessarily driving an extra 3.5 million kilometres in his district every year because bridges are not up to scratch and the council will soon have to weigh up reverting sealed roads to gravel.

But South Island Minister James Meager says the government has made a huge investment in the South Island's roads and other infrastructure, as well as simplifying and speeding up consent processes and cutting red tape.

It was "simplistic" to suggest the government was not listening to the South Island's leaders and delivering on their priorities, Meager said.

The report, released on Thursday and commissioned by the South Island Regional Transport Committee Chairs Group, highlighted the disparity between the south's contribution to the economy and what was being delivered by the National Land Transport Fund.

If National Land Transport Fund expenditure matched the population in the South Island it would have resulted in an extra $1.2 billion in spending in the past year alone -about the cost of the currently unfunded Woodend Bypass or the Hope Bypass.

South Island Minister James Meager RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

"That's a fair point," Meager said.

"I guess my response would be is that it's a little more complex than just looking at the population makeup. It's actually part of my job, and part of my colleagues' jobs, to make sure that we raise these issues with decision makers, with cabinet, and making sure that we've got the investment in the right place.

"The key thing is we need to not necessarily look at writing checks based on what the population is here or there. What we need to do ... is to identify the infrastructure constraints that we have in the South Island that actually are holding back growth.

"And we have got a lot of stuff underway. We can't underestimate all the work that actually is happening. You've got Ashburton Bridge. The Woodend Bypass is proceeding - just got consenting, just got fast-track consent. In the budget there was $400 million for roading infrastructure resilience and $140 million of that went to the South Island. So there is a lot happening."

'It's keeping us awake at night'

RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Canterbury Regional Transport Committee chair Deon Swiggs said the report highlighted what many in the South Island had been feeling for some time.

"When I look at the numbers it's disappointing ... and resilience is the big piece that we are fighting for in the South Island," Swiggs said.

"We've got storm events that are happening, we've got ageing infrastructure. So, yes, the South Island is definitely punching above its weight from an economic activity point of view and the money generated here is going towards New Zealand at large, but the South Island needs this investment.

"We've been saying this for quite some time that the numbers do not stack up ... and investment in the South Island needs to improve. We do not want to see the degradation of our existing corridors. We all know that when you don't maintain what you've got, it costs a lot more to then fix it."

Rob Scott said Southland was at a tipping point.

"I've seen the great work that our staff have been doing and I'm seeing the stress coming through now and it's keeping us awake at night as a council, knowing that once we get over that tipping point we're not going to be able to recover as a Southland region and also as a country. It's going to be a lot more expensive to fix the roads up later on ... rather than just actually keeping on top and maintaining our network properly," he said.

"If you look at the length of road per capita that people are looking after, in Auckland a resident is looking after four metres worth of road. Wellington, 1.6 metres. And if we come to the South Island and we've got our fastest growing district in the country at the moment, Selwyn, someone's looking after 30 metres. What do you reckon Southland's number is? It's 151 metres.

"We are subsidising Auckland, which I don't mind, but it's actually coming at the expense of our roads. All of the road user charges that we generate on our roads, only half of that is coming back for that road maintenance."

Rob Scott. Matthew Rosenberg / LDR

It led him to write a letter to Transport Agency chair Simon Bridges calling for a new way of allocating road funding as Southland was tens of millions of dollars short of just maintaining the status quo.

Meanwhile central government was pushing ahead with further expressways and highways that would put even more pressure on maintenance spending, Scott said.

"If the heartbeat of New Zealand's export market loses the routes to get that produce to market, we're going to be in trouble as a country," he said.

"We're not actually asking for much. I scratch my head when I see all of this money - that $55 million going onto that Harbour Bridge Extension paperwork, the $250 million going on a [Queenstown] roundabout, the new 26 kilometres worth of expressway in the North Island - we just need a drop in the bucket from all of those projects just to be able to maintain our roads."

'We have two Cabinet ministers in the whole of the South Island'

Swiggs said politics was at play.

"What we're seeing here is that there is a weighting of North Island politicians and less South Island politicians and especially in Cabinet. I think we have two politicians in Cabinet from the South Island," Swiggs said.

"We need to have a better mix of proportionality around the politicians that are decision makers at Cabinet. But we also need a more transparent process about how the money has been apportioned and where these big projects are."

Local councils had to be far more transparent in how they decided to spend money compared to central government, Swiggs said.

Business Canterbury chief executive Leeann Watson agreed South Island representation was lacking among senior politicians.

"We are underrepresented, absolutely. We have two cabinet ministers in the whole of the South Island and I believe Auckland has 16. So that in itself speaks some volume," she said.

Despite that Business Canterbury had regular contact with Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour and Finance Minister Nicola Willis, Watson said.

Willis claimed after this year's budget she had not "had a request for a major headline project in Canterbury".

Luxon offered a similar view last year and called for Canterbury's leaders to get their priorities straight.

Watson said the remarks were frustrating.

"There is no doubt that we have asked for some investment," she said.

Business Canterbury chief executive Leeann Watson. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Swiggs said there was "no shortage of projects that we could do tomorrow to make the South Island a better place".

"I'm going to pick on one, which is the long-touted mass rapid transit for Christchurch. Mass rapid transit is an end goal," he said.

"To get to the mass rapid transit system we need to do the investment in our existing public transport. We've put through business cases to NZTA. This council appropriated the money through our long-term plan. We went through consultation. We had it on our budgets and then the [Government Policy Statement] comes out and cut the funding.

"That has a flow-on effect to us not being able to deliver the improvements to our public transport that we wanted and then that has an impact on the mass rapid transit down the line. When the government puts a cap on what the region wants or the city wants it has flow-on effects.

"That was there and that could be delivered relatively quickly if there was a will from the government and ... they have that information. So that's just one example. They could invest in that with us, with the region, with the city, but they've chosen not to."

Meager said the government was committed to delivering the Woodend Bypass.

"We're not short on ambition. What we are short on is, quite frankly, the revenue needed to get these projects across the line," he said.

"Now part of that is to do with the growth we need to generate revenue, whether that's through fuel excise and road users which help fund the land transport fund or general growth.

"So we need more revenue coming in. We also need to make these projects a lot more affordable and a lot cheaper and so that's why we've done things like Fast-track and reforming the RMA system so that when these large scale projects are actually underway, we can make them more affordable."

There was a significant amount taking place in and around Canterbury, including the recently opened Te Kaha Stadium in Christchurch, flood protection improvement and spending in health, education and transport, Meager said.

'The South Island is outperforming the North Island'

The report laid bare what has been described as New Zealand's "two-speed" economy.

"The South Island is outperforming the North Island with GDP growing by 1.2 percent in the March 2026 year compared with 0.2 percent in the North Island," the report said.

South Island economic snapshot Supplied/Benje Patterson

"This outperformance has persisted, with South Island GDP growth averaging 0.6 percentage points above the North Island over the five years to 2025.

"South Island employment rose by 0.4 percent, while North Island employment fell by 1.2 percent. Southland, the West Coast, Canterbury and Otago recorded growth. The South Island's unemployment rate is 4.1 percent, below the North Island's 5.7 percent."

The South Island was making an outsized contribution to the country's economy but further investment was important to maintain it, the report said.

The roading network was vital to connect people and businesses with supply chains and markets and for tourism.

The South Island accounted for 43 percent of the country's roading network and 45 percent of the State Highway network.

"The South Island's share of roading expenditure appears disproportionately low relative to its contribution and level of road use. In 2025 the South Island received 11 percent of NLTF roading expenditure despite generating 27 percent of national vehicle kilometres travelled, 22 percent of GDP, one third of goods exports, and 40 percent of international visitor spending," the report said.

"This imbalance is evident across South Island regions, where shares of population, GDP, exports, visitor spending and road use generally exceed each region's share of NLTF roading investment. Ensuring that South Island transport infrastructure is adequately maintained and invested in is therefore important not only for the South Island but for New Zealand's overall economic performance."

The report also underscored the importance of the Cook Strait ferries to the South Island's economy.

"The Cook Strait ferries provide a 'sea bridge' connection between the South Island and the North Island. The transportation infrastructure provided by the ferries is a critically important economic enabler for the South Island economy and its broader contribution to New Zealand.

"An estimated 3.5 million tonnes of annual freight are carried on ferries."

More than $10 billion crossed the strait last year with 71 percent southbound and 29 percent northbound.

About $1.8 billion of South Island international spending came from visitors who took the ferry.

"This is equivalent to about 23 percent of the total international visitor spending that occurred in the South Island over the past year, which highlights the critical importance of the ferries as an enabler of international tourism earnings. Transport connectivity is fundamental to sustaining this contribution."

South Island road funding Supplied/Benje Patterson

Back the South Island for stronger productivity and higher incomes - business leaders

Watson said the government needed to be investing more in the South Island's infrastructure for the good of the country's economy.

"We can have the best innovation, we can have the best quality products, but if we haven't got the infrastructure to support the imported components coming in to make those manufactured goods or the right roads to get our exports to Lyttelton Port or to Christchurch Airport or not sufficient freight capacity then ... we can't actually realise the full potential of those exports to this country," she said.

"Infrastructure is vital, just like energy is. It underpins everything that we do from moving our people, moving our freight and just having connectivity across the South Island.

"Our message to political parties is really simple - if New Zealand wants stronger productivity and higher incomes and greater resilience then backing the South Island right now is exactly what they should be doing because we can provide all that with the right settings."

The government could not afford to not invest in the south, Watson said.

"We often talk about what the costs are of delivering projects but we don't talk about the cost of delaying and deferring," she said.

"First of all, I think we've got to do a better job of actually costing up the project. Secondly, I think we need to look at those alternative procurement and funding and financing models because we know if we continue to use the same funding and financing and the same procurement models that we've always used, we'll get what we've always got.

"Right now we've got a country that has definitely got some resilience issues in terms of some of its core infrastructure. We've got a whole lot of maintenance that we need to do and so we've got to make sure that we also look at those alternative ways of doing things."

Watson and Swiggs emphasised that funding infrastructure in the South Island was an investment.

Swiggs said money spent in the South Island benefited the whole country.

"This is definitely not a handout. We have shown where the money has been generated, we've shown the economic activity is happening here," Swiggs said.

Watson said Business Canterbury was working on a project called Canterbury Ambition that set out the region's vision for improving growth, innovation and quality of life.

She said that, alongside government investment, could unlock the private sector.

"In some cases it's actually about getting the government out of the way," she said.

"The piece of work around Canterbury Ambition is actually about not waiting for government to tell us what we should be as a region or what we should do. It's about us shaping our own future. So the private sector is in the driving seat of that and actually pushing ahead and what we've heard from this government is that they actually want to partner with business.

World.title: Aussie star completes major move to EPL after breakout World Cup
World.content:
Socceroos teenager Lucas Herrington has completed his move to English Premier League side Hull City.

The 18-year-old defender, who announced himself on the international stage with an impressive performance for Australia at the FIFA World Cup, has been signed from US club Colorado Rapids for an undisclosed fee.

Herrington has agreed to a five-year contract with the Tigers, who were promoted to the Premier League after winning the English Championship play-off final against Middlesbrough in May.

"The opportunity to play in the Premier League, one of the best leagues in the world, is a dream come true," Herrington said in a statement.

"I've woken up at all hours in the morning in Australia to watch these games. To be a part of it is so special.

"To hear from the club and coaching staff has been so exciting for me. I can't wait to meet all the boys and the fans. I'm here to work hard and hopefully get a lot of games in the Premier League."

Herrington, born in Brisbane, made his A-League debut for Brisbane Roar in December 2024.

He played 29 matches for the Roar before moving to Colorado.

Hull begins its Premier League campaign with a home match against Manchester United on August 22.

World.title: Teenager breaks Kaylee McKeown's backstroke world record
World.content:
Italian teenager Sara Curtis has set a new world record in the women's 50m backstroke, beating the mark previously held by Australian great Kaylee McKeown.

Curtis smashed the Queenslander's 50m global mark in 26.63 seconds ‌during the semifinals of the European championships in the ‌Paris Olympic pool on Wednesday, local time.

That slashed nearly a whopping quarter-of-a-second off McKeown's mark of 26.86 set at a World Cup meet in Budapest, Hungary, in October 2023.

Curtis, born in Savigliano to an Italian father and a Nigerian mother, has been making dramatic strides since attending the swimming powerhouse University of Virginia.

She had signalled her form by winning bronze in Tuesday's 100m freestyle at the Europeans, but she was stunned by her record-breaking swim.

"I knew I was capable of doing it, but I didn't expect it here, in this race, in this moment," the youngster beamed.

"It's just so awesome, and I'm so happy! I can tell that I am superwoman right now, it's unbelievable, and I don't think I'm going to be able to sleep tonight."

There were other warning signs for 25-year-old Queenslander McKeown, with Russian Alina Gaifutdinova coming home ‌second-fastest in the semifinals in 26.91, the third-fastest time in history.

When McKeown recorded her 50m time in 2023, she was the first swimmer to hold the 50, 100 and ‌200m backstroke world records simultaneously.

Now, though, McKeown only holds the 200m mark after losing the 100m record to US rival Regan Smith in June ⁠2024.

McKeown, a five-time Olympic champion, is recovering from glandular fever that forced her out of the Commonwealth Games and this week's Pan Pacific Championships.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Messi doubts playing 'for much longer' after father's death
World.content:
Football legend Lionel Messi doubts his playing career will last "much longer" following the recent death of his father.

Jorge Messi passed away on Saturday at the age of 68 after being hospitalised during this summer's FIFA World Cup.

Lionel Messi, 39, posted a statement on social media on Wednesday, local time, saying he "does not know how to carry on".

"All I ever did was play football, and now I have a fair few doubts as to whether I'll carry on doing it for much longer," the Inter Miami forward wrote.

"You were by my side from the start, we were so close to the end (of his career). Why didn't you hang on just that little bit longer so we could finish it together?"

Messi, an eight-time Ballon d'Or winner as the world's greatest player, is currently in his fourth season with Miami. He led the team to its first MLS Cup championship and won his second straight league MVP award last season.

The Argentina native is under contract with Inter Miami through 2028, earning a reported base salary of $US25 million ($34.5 million) per campaign.

His father played a significant role in his son's development and professional career, having served as his agent and business manager.

Here is the full text of Messi's emotional post:

"Dad, I still can't believe you're gone. I can't get my head round it — or rather, I don't want to. It's so hard for me to imagine that I won't see you ever again, that we won't talk anymore," the Inter Miami star wrote.

"I know you were suffering and that this is for the best, but you left us far too soon. We still had so much left to enjoy together.

"You kept asking me to play in the last World Cup, and it was just days before it started that you took a turn for the worse. It was the first time you weren't going to be at a tournament, but Mum kept telling me you'd get better and that you'd be well enough to travel. I'd tell you that we'd make it to the final so you could travel.

"Every time a match ended, I'd wait for your message and miss it. That's when I realised the situation was really bad. Even so, I couldn't stop thinking about getting as far as possible, to give you time to watch a match. We reached the final and you couldn't be there. I wanted to win it so I could take it to you and show you another trophy. I couldn't do it, my legs wouldn't carry me any further. This time I tried to go against my physical limits, but I couldn't. I never managed to feel right.

"When I got back, you thought we'd lost the final on penalties. We couldn't talk about any of what had happened. You couldn't enjoy any of it. We didn't win the title, but you have no idea how much we enjoyed every match. Once again, you were right: I had to be there and play.

"I'm telling you this because it was the only thing we couldn't talk about, because you already know all the rest. We spoke every day and saw each other whenever we could, depending on my commitments.

"I don't know what I'm going to do without you, I don't know how to carry on. All I ever did was play football, and now I have a fair few doubts as to whether I'll carry on doing it for much longer. You were by my side from the start, we were so close to the end (of his career). Why didn't you hang on just that little bit longer so we could finish it together?

"I know that your happiness came from seeing your family doing well — your wife and your children, and above all, without the others finding out, watching me play … (winking emoji)

"Ever since I was a little boy, it was always like that. You'd take me to every training session as soon as you got home from work. Mum used to take me to a lot of them because you were working.

"Of course, you never missed a single match. How you suffered watching me and how you enjoyed it, even though you never showered me with praise.

"You were a dad, a friend and a representative. You were always the person you needed to be at every moment, and you never got anything wrong. Despite the odd reproach or argument, you were always right. In the end, things always turned out as you said they would.

"I'm going to miss you so much, but you'll always be present, and above all in bringing up my children, because I'm teaching and raising them as you both did with me.

"Rest in peace and look after us from up there, just as you did here. Thank you for everything.

"I love you, dad."

World.title: Bazball-era curfews over as Root demands England players 'be adults'
World.content:
England skipper Joe Root says the midnight curfews in place at the end of the Bazball reign have been ditched as he called on his players to "be adults" in the new era.

With another Ashes series on the horizon in England next summer, Root has launched his second spell as Test captain with the message that his team need to remember: "You're playing for England."

Root's new reign at the age of 35 starts at Headingley next Wednesday against Pakistan in a three-Test series, which will be the first since Ben Stokes retired from international cricket and Brendon McCullum lost his job as Test coach in a turbulent spell.

Stokes claims cricket has drinking culture Ben Stokes defends his former teammates by saying the sport of cricket as a whole has an unhealthy relationship with alcohol.

In an interview with former captain Mike Atherton on Sky Sports Cricket Podcast, Root was asked if the player curfew, which was breached by Stokes and quick Gus Atkinson in a post-midnight nightclub incident in June, was still going to be in place.

"There's not going to be a curfew. I don't think this needs to be a big deal, to be honest," Root said.

"My view on curfews is I don't think they work, and if you want guys to take responsibility on the field they've got to be able to feel they can be grown adults off it and make good strong decisions off it.

"That's for us as a team to manage well, and self-police well, for me and Flem (new coach Stephen Fleming) to manage well in many ways.

Ben Stokes's retirement a perfect example of his main character energy Ben Stokes has been the centre of England's cricketing universe for 15 years. In announcing his retirement mid-match, he highlighted how damaging that main character energy can be.

"But ultimately you're grown adults, you know what it takes to play for England, you know what your responsibilities are off the field, and we need to make sure we don't find ourselves with any little situations off the field.

"We should be known for how we play our cricket and what we do on the field. We should be on the back pages of the newspapers and people reading about that sort of stuff.

"Be adults, look after yourselves, look after each other, create a good strong culture when you know when the right time is to celebrate and enjoy a win or to have a sensible beer or whatever, but remember you're playing for England."

The curfew had been instituted by England men's managing director Rob Key in the aftermath of the pre-Ashes tour to New Zealand last November when Harry Brook was fined for an altercation with a nightclub bouncer on the eve of an ODI in Wellington.

England players' behaviour was then put under the spotlight during their 4-1 Ashes hammering, with opener Ben Duckett admitting he was not proud of being caught on camera under the influence of alcohol when they were 2-0 down in the series.

AAP

World.title: Binders can be 'life-changing' for trans people. But are they safe to exercise in?
World.content:
AFLW player Tilly Lucas-Rodd remembers the "trans joy" they felt the first time they wore a chest binder.

"It was incredible," they said.

"It was so relieving … I remember I put a T-shirt on, and I was like, 'this is life-changing.'"

GWS player Lucas-Rodd is non-binary, and has since had top surgery, a procedure that involves the removal of breast tissue. They have spoken openly to the ABC about how the gender-affirming operation brought their body in line with how they had "always seen [themselves] internally".

Before top surgery, Lucas-Rodd relied on chest binders to reduce gender dysphoria — a psychological term used to describe the distress that can arise when someone experiences a "mismatch" between their gender identity and the sex they were assigned with at birth.

Binding is common among trans men, non-binary and masculine-identifying people who were assigned female at birth.

Tilly Lucas-Rodd wants to share their gender identity journey to help others who can relate. (Getty: Emily Barker)

Anecdotally, however, binding can also have unwanted side-effects, including discomfort, pain, overheating, breathing restrictions, skin irritation and more. Many trans and gender diverse people also believe it may be harmful to bind while exercising, a fear Lucas-Rodd shared.

They experienced skin chafing and "scarring" under their armpits from a string of ill-fitting binders and took to the internet to try and find information on binding while playing sport.

"There wasn't a lot of research," they said.

"But my need and desire to bind kind of outweighed [my fears].

"I was like, I feel so uncomfortable that I'll take some of those negative side effects if they happen."

Australian researchers are now trying to close the gap on a lack of knowledge about binding and exercise, with preliminary results from one study led by the Mental Health and Exercise Research Group at the University of Western Australia (UWA), providing some reassurance.

Loading Instagram content

Largest study yet finds 'comforting' preliminary results

The UWA-led project, done in conjunction with Curtin University, The University of New South Wales, The Kids Research Institute and Thriving in Motion, studied a group of 21 people who were assigned female at birth to see if there were any significant differences between exercising with or without a binder.

No-one in the group had previously worn a chest binder, and all were issued a commercial binder by researchers who had been trained in correct fitting.

Participants took part in two separate exercise sessions — one with and one without a binder — and were put through tests to assess their aerobic fitness, muscle strength and lung function amongst other measures.

Participants in the study were put through tests with and without wearing a binder. (Supplied: UWA)

Researchers found no significant differences when participants were wearing or not wearing a binder, a finding PhD candidate Kai Schweizer says helps dispel the "non-evidence based" perception that binding while exercising is unsafe.

"The findings are really interesting and somewhat comforting," he said.

"We don't have enough evidence to say anything with certainty yet, but our sample was — believe it or not — the largest collected in this area so far.

"Our research is not a definitive answer but it's the first step in trying to better understand the impact of binding on exercise."

As Schweizer explains it, trans and gender diverse people already participate in sport and physical activity at much lower rates than the general population.

PhD candidate Kai Schweizer says the research doesn't give definitive answers, but it's a step closer to understanding the impacts. (Supplied)

"That then contributes to the really high disparities in things like cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes and osteoporosis," Schweizer explains.

"One of the barriers to exercise we identified was the perception among trans folk that it was unsafe to exercise in a chest binder.

"Hopefully this research inspires further, more detailed, bigger studies so that we can try and reduce barriers for trans and gender diverse people to exercise."

One limitation of the UWA study is that they only studied the impacts of binding in the short-term.

However, Schweizer points to a pilot study conducted last year, which followed a group of eighteen trans and gender diverse teenagers, most of whom had been binding for over a year, and found that wearing a binder did not impact exercise capacity.

"We'll need more longitudinal data to really answer the safety question, but I was glad to see that other researchers had started looking at this and their findings didn't substantially differ from ours," he added.

Lucas-Rodd felt 'trans-joy' the first time they wore a binder. (Getty Images: Mark Evans)

The importance of finding the right fit

The findings of the Australian study, which are currently under peer-review, come as welcome news to Adam Brownhill, medical director of a gender-affirming care clinic in Melbourne.

"A healthy lifestyle is an important lifestyle, so anything we find or learn that helps improve inclusion and participation in sport is really, really important," Dr Brownhill said.

"This is a really reassuring piece of research, in that there was no harm found."

Dr Brownhill does, however, emphasise the importance of finding the right type of binder, and correct fit, to ensure safety while exercising.

He says DIY methods like taping can damage the skin if done repeatedly, and cause harm.

"It's like anything — a pair of glasses, a bra, a pair of shoes — you need to make sure it fits properly when you're using it."

Finding the right fit is essential when looking for a binder to exercise in. (Supplied)

There are several custom binding manufacturers in Australia, including Sock Drawer Heroes — who supplied the binders worn in the UWA study — and Transform Transwear, a Melbourne-based company created by Simone Kelly.

Kelly's stepson Eli came out as trans seven years ago but was unable to find any binders available for sale in Australia. Kelly says she was forced to order items from overseas for Eli that were expensive, took a long time to arrive, and were "cheaply made" and "poorly designed".

The experience left her "sad and angry" and fuelled her passion to provide a physical space where trans and gender diverse people could be fitted safely and in private. Since opening their Melbourne-based store in 2024, Transform have serviced clients like Lucas-Rodd, and recently released a binder designed specifically for swimming.

Simone Kelly (right) opened Transform Transwear so that people looking for binders could be fitted properly. (Supplied)

"We get people coming in for swimwear and talking about how long it has been since they've been able to swim," Kelly said.

"Someone came in recently and said, 'I used to love surfing with my Dad as a kid, but I haven't done it in such a long time. So I'm really excited to get out and surf with my Dad.'

"We know young people getting out there and exercising is really fantastic for their mental health, but many are consumed by their dysphoria and don't feel comfortable enough to go and do things like that."

While Kelly acknowledges that the preliminary findings of the UWA study are only the beginning, she says research like it is critical for trans and gender diverse people's health.

"Right up until this research came out, we were telling our customers, don't exercise in a binder and don't sleep in a binder," she said.

"Obviously we need to do more research to help give us more detailed guidance, but this is a great start. It's a step in the right direction."

World.title: The Kiss era has begun, and new coach Les is seeking the 'Wallaby way'
World.content:
The new Wallabies era began with a win in tough conditions against an improving nation, but coach Les Kiss wants more than just wins to be the legacy of his tenure.

The Wallabies head to the Queensland city of Townsville this Saturday for the second and final Test against Japan, after being pushed all the way in Osaka by the Brave Blossoms last weekend.

With the anticipation of Kiss's first match in charge in the rear-view mirror, the former Queensland and Australia rugby league representative is now plotting the Wallabies' bid for success at a home Rugby World Cup late next year.

Wallabies survive scare as Kiss era begins with win New Wallabies coach Les Kiss says his side will need to learn how to control their ambitions after Australia hangs on to win a frantic Test match against Japan in the Osaka heat.

The next step is this Saturday against Japan, the first match between the two nations on Australian soil in 39 years.

But Kiss is seeking more than just Test match victories. He wants the current group of Wallabies to play with a passion that embodies pride, passion and the Australian spirit.

The new Australian boss spoke on ABC Radio Sydney on Wednesday morning, where he outlined what he hoped to foster during his tenure.

"One thing I don’t want to miss in this whole journey is to find a Wallaby way that they are really proud of and blaze their own trail," Kiss said.

"We’ve had some great Wallaby teams in the past; they should be inspiring us and we should empower this group to blaze a trail and make a Wallabies’ way that his their way."

Wallaby fans got a glimpse into the culture Kiss wants to instil when he was captured on the television broadcast having a laugh in the coaching box during the second half of last weekend's three-point win over Japan.

Asked about that moment, Kiss said it was a brief moment where humour was able to ease the tension during a hard-fought Test.

"It shouldn’t all be just a frown … or that your head’s so deep in something that you can’t enjoy the process as well," he told ABC Radio Sydney.

"I think that’s part of the Aussie spirit. We’re competitive, we’ll fight for anything, but we’ll have a crack and a bit of fun along the way.

"This means a lot to me. I know there is a lot at stake for the game here.

"We want to make sure we can do the right thing to continue to grow that game."

Kiss's desire for his players to enjoy the privilege of being a Wallaby appears to be rubbing off.

Angus Bell came off the bench during last week's win over Japan. (Getty Images: Paul Miller)

Prop Angus Bell, a second-generation Wallaby, told media on Wednesday that Kiss has focused on ensuring each player embraces each opportunity to represent Australia.

"Week to week, you get sort of caught in the washing machine of what Test match rugby is. You're always bashing each other, trying to get better at training and you get lost in how special a Test match is," Bell said.

"Test matches don't come around often; people don't get many caps.

"So I think what Les touches on is how special it is if you get the opportunity in the [team], how awesome it is, because one day it all stops.

"He's really just instilled in us how actually special it is to represent the Wallabies."

On the field, Kiss has some decisions to make about who plays in Townsville on Saturday afternoon.

Lock Miles Amatosero was handed a three-match suspension after being red-carded for head contact in a breakdown, opening up a starting spot in the middle row.

Joseph-Aukuso Sua'ali'i was ruled out earlier this week after suffering hamstring soreness, with Italy-bound Josh Flook coming into the squad.

Queensland Reds prop Massimo De Lutiis has also been brought into the squad, and could be in line to make his international debut if selected on Thursday. Should De Lutiis be picked and play on Saturday, he would become the 1,000th Wallaby.

Following last week's win over Japan, and a 57-10 triumph over Italy last month, the Wallabies are attempting to win three Tests in a row for the first time in two years.

ABC Sport will have live blog coverage of the second Test between the Wallabies and Japan on Saturday afternoon from 2pm AEST.

World.title: Ex-Wallabies, league star Brian Smith dies of cancer
World.content:
Wallabies prop Angus Bell is leading the tributes for dual rugby union international and former NRL star Brian Smith, who has died aged 59.

Smith, who played six Tests for Australia in 1987 and nine for Ireland after switching allegiance, had battled cancer.

Once described by former Wallabies coach Alan Jones as one of the world's most gifted players, Smith was most recently the Head of Sport at Scots College in Sydney, where Bell and many other Wallabies graduated from.

"He was coaching at the Scots school and coached a lot of us coming through the grades and I just wanted to say it's a really sad time," Bell said from Wallabies camp in Townsville on Wednesday.

"We're wishing the best for his wife and kids. He's an avid rugby person and helped a lot of individuals in the squad and in the Wallabies today, so just sending my condolences from both the Wallabies and myself."

Australia's 999th Wallaby's Test debut Isaac Henry will run the prospect of fresh ink past his wife but is otherwise assured he can make a permanent Wallabies mark after a hard-earned debut in Osaka.

Smith, who also played 43 games for Balmain and Eastern Suburbs from 1991 to 1994, coached Bell at GPS and NSW schoolboys' level when the emerging front-rower was only 16.

"Fair to say that I wouldn't have played as good or anywhere near as good without him," Bell said.

"Me, Jeremy Williams and Will Harris from the (Western) Force were really close with him and he was a great bloke, a great father and a great coach.

"So, yeah, very sad."

After playing schoolboys' rugby for Australia, Smith made his Wallabies debut under Jones in 1987, partnering Nick Farr-Jones in the halves and bagging 18 points from a try, five conversions and a penalty in a 65-18 win over South Korea.

Australian forward Angus Bell - in Wallabies camp in Townsville - paid tribute to his former high school coach and mentor Brian Smith. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

After his playing career, Smith coached in Japan and England, where he was the national team's attack coach, and served as Australia's sevens coach.

"Brian had been very unwell in recent months and was battling an aggressive cancer," Scots College principal Dr Ian PM Lambert wrote to school colleagues.

"This is very sad news for our College community and I know it will come as a shock to many of you who knew and worked closely with him.

"Our immediate thoughts are with Brian's wife Lisa, his daughters Ruby and Santana, and his son Chilli."

AAP

World.title: Former Hurricanes cricketer jailed for abusing 15yo girl
World.content:
A former Hobart Hurricanes cricket player will serve 10 months in prison for sexually abusing a child.

WARNING: This story contains details of child sexual abuse.

Aaron William Summers, 30, pleaded guilty to two counts of penetrative sexual abuse of a young person and one count of grooming in June in the Supreme Court of Tasmania, after having previously pleaded not guilty.

In court on Wednesday, he was sentenced to two-and-a-half years in jail, suspended after 10 months, meaning he will leave prison in April next year.

Justice Helen Wood told the court that Summers met the victim at a Hobart Hurricanes cricket match in 2017.

The following month, the 15-year-old girl attended another game and spoke to Summers, who was 21 at the time.

Aaron Summers was playing for the Hobart Hurricanes when he met the 15-year-old girl. (Getty Images: Robert Prezioso)

The pair began messaging on social media, and Summers arranged to pick her up from her home later that night.

The court heard he drove her to a local primary school, laid down a blanket, and sexually abused her twice.

Justice Wood told the court that Summers knew she was under the age of 17 and at high school, but did not ask how old she was.

"She thought they were meeting to talk; in reality, she represented a sexual opportunity to him," Justice Wood said.

"She was vulnerable because of her age and innocence; he had said nothing to warn her of his real motives."

The grooming charge related to social media conversations between Summers and the girl, in which Summers sent explicit photos of himself and requested photos from her.

"As a community, we look up to sportspeople; young people are likely to admire them, see them in a positive light," Justice Woods said.

"His role as a sportsperson gave him contact with young people, and enabled the commission of his crimes; this is an aggravating factor."

In November 2021, Summers pleaded guilty to charges in the Northern Territory, including possessing and transmitting child abuse material and transmitting communication with someone under 16 with the intention of procuring the recipient to engage in, or make, sexual activity.

Summers served three years and 11 months in prison in the NT. He was arrested on the day of his release and extradited to Tasmania to face these charges.

Cricket career 'at an end'

Justice Wood said Summers had experienced social isolation, loneliness and depressive symptoms while playing cricket in Tasmania and was spending excessive time on social media.

She said once he moved to the Northern Territory, he had established a successful career playing cricket in Australia and overseas and had a high profile.

"Due to the crimes, his future as a professional cricketer is at an end," she said.

Twenty months of the sentence was suspended, meaning Aaron Summers (left) is set for release in April next year. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Justice Wood said that Summers has accepted responsibility for his crimes and understood the impact his offending has had on his victims.

In the NT, he completed an intensive sex offender treatment program, which involved over 100 sessions, in which Justice Wood told the court he engaged appropriately and gained insight into his offending.

Justice Wood said when deciding on his sentence, she considered the lengthy jail time he had already served in the NT after the Tasmanian crimes were committed, and the significant progress he has taken towards his rehabilitation.

"[The] understanding he has about the harm he has caused and he is motivated to regain his life," she said.

Justice Wood imposed a sentence of two-and-a-half years, backdated to June 28 of this year, due to the time he has spent in remand.

She suspended the last 20 months of the sentence, with strict conditions, such as obliging him to comply with his probation officers and submit to psychological treatment.

The court heard that Summers would likely return to Western Australia, where he is from and his family live, to serve out his suspended sentence once he is able to leave prison in April next year.

Tech.title: Cats and dogs are missing meals after a popular smart feeder went down
Tech.content:
A Petlibro outage is preventing its smart pet feeders and other devices from performing scheduled tasks, like dispensing food. The outage began on Tuesday, with users across Reddit reporting that their smart feeders, litter boxes, and water fountains have gone offline .

“We are currently experiencing a service issue affecting some Petlibro app functions,” Petlibro said on Tuesday. “Our team is actively restoring service, validating stability, and bringing functionality back in stages.” In an update on Wednesday at 2:30PM ET, Petlibro said that “much of our service is restored as we continue to bring the app back into full operation.” Some users say their devices have started working again, but others are still having issues reconnecting them to the Petlibro app.

Tech.title: The next big indie game publisher is taking some exciting swings
Tech.content:
Players take on the role of Diana, a woman who discovers she can receive visions of the future after an experimental implant is embedded into her brain.

Players will be tasked with exploring these visions of the future, focusing on specific moments and committing them to Diana’s memory in the present day. Prescience comes with consequences, however, and as soon as Diana commits a detail to memory, the very future ahead of her changes.

Tech.title: It looks like Apple’s iPhone 18 really will skip the fall launch this year
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

According to an Economic Daily News report spotted by MacRumors, executives for Apple supplier Pegatron confirmed during an earnings call that the iPhone 18 Pro series phones will launch this fall, but the base iPhone 18 won’t arrive until the first quarter of next year. The more affordable iPhone 18e and a new iPhone Air are also rumored to launch around the same time, in line with rumors that have been circulating for more than a year.

Analyst Ming-Chi Kuo and The Information both reported last year that Apple was planning to only launch its premium iPhones in fall 2026, and earlier this year another Apple supplier said one of its customers was postponing a phone launch to early 2027.

Along with the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple’s rumored “Ultra” foldable is reportedly launching this fall. The EDN report cites Pegatron execs saying that memory and chip shortages are causing the peak shipping seasons to shift, as its customers like Apple figure out how to spread out the parts they have and increasingly prioritize higher-priced models that have larger margins.

Tech.title: Google’s Pixel 11 phone preorders come with up to $350 in gift cards
Tech.content:
Brad Bourque is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Looking to get your hands on the latest Pixel devices? After weeks of leaks and rumors, Google has officially announced its next generation of Pixel phones and watches.

The base Pixel 11 starts at $899, the Pro and Pro XL are $1,099 and $1,299 respectively, and the Pro Fold starts at $1,899. The watch comes in two sizes, with the smaller 41mm model starting at $399, and the larger 45mm model starting at $429. The phones are available for preorder now, and will ship on August 20th, 2026.

If you’re looking to preorder an unlocked phone on its own, your main options are Best Buy, Amazon, and directly from the Google Store. All three are running a similar introductory deal, where you’ll receive a gift card for a future purchase at that retailer, with the value depending on which model you buy. The Pixel 11 includes a $100 gift card, the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL include a $200 gift card, and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold includes a $350 gift card. Only Google lists an end date for the promotion, which is August 27th, 2026.

If you’d also like a Pixel Watch 5, Google and Amazon will give you additional credit towards that purchase instead of the gift card. The Pixel 11 and 41mm watch bundle is $1,168.99, effectively a $130 discount if you bought the two devices separately, but only in obsidian. The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL with a 41mm watch as a bundle is discounted by $250. The Amazon bundles include only the Wi-Fi versions of the Pixel Watch 5 and only in limited color combinations. The Google store will let you apply the credit to other in-stock variants. If you buy a Pixel 11 Pro Fold, you can opt for a 41mm Wi-Fi watch for free, with Amazon offering obsidian only and Google letting you choose your colors.

Each phone is powered by the new Tensor G6 processor, which Google says is capable of 25 percent faster web browsing and 15 percent improvement to app loading speeds over the Tensor G5. The camera and video features are a focus of the new Pixel 11 series phones. The new Magic Capture feature lets you forget about snapping a great shot, and instead stitches together a series of clips and photos from a longer video. All four phones also featuring upgraded batteries and fast charging, with wireless charging support for Qi2.2 up to 25W.

If you’re deciding which Pixel is right for you, make sure to check out our initial hands-on impressions for the new Pixel 11 series phones and the Pixel Watch 5.

Where to preorder the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL

The Pixel 11 Pro starts at $1,099 for the base model with 256GB of storage, and goes up to $1,219 for the 512GB model, or $1,449 for the 1TB model. The larger Pixel 11 Pro XL starts at $1,299 for the 256GB configuration, with the 512GB costing $1,419 and the 1TB model priced at $1,649. For both phones, the 256GB version has 12GB of memory, while the larger capacity models have 16GB of memory.

Apart from the screen size, resolution, and battery capacity, the two phones are otherwise identical to each other. They feature updated cameras, including a 50MP wide angle, 48MP telephoto with up to 5x optical zoom, a 48MP ultrawide sensor, and a 42MP selfie camera with a 103 degree field of view. The phones are available in four colors: canyon, fog, olive, and obsidian.

Where to preorder the Pixel 11

The Pixel 11 starts at $899 for the model with 256GB of storage, and the price rising to $1,019 for the 512GB model, both of which have 12GB of memory. The 6.3-inch display has a 1080 x 2424 resolution and 60-120Hz refresh rate, with HDR support up to 2000 nits, or 3000 nit brightness with HDR off. For cameras, the Pixel 11 sports a 48MP sensor wide camera, a 13MP ultrawide, a 10.8 MP telephoto with 5x optical zoom, and a 10.5MP selfie camera with a 95 degree field of view. The phone is available in four colors: frost, pistachio, hibiscus, and obsidian.

Where to preorder the Pixel 11 Pro Fold

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold starts at $1,899 for the base model with 256GB and 16GB of RAM, with a 512GB model for $2,019, and a 1TB option for $2,249 available as well. It’s available in two colors: olive and obsidian.

The only foldable phone in Google’s Pixel lineup, the 11 Pro Fold features a 6.5-inch external display, and a 8-inch internal display when opened. Both screens feature refresh rates up to 120Hz, and HDR support. The internal and front selfie cameras are 10MP sensors, and the main camera block features a 10.5MP ultrawide, 10.8MP telephoto with up to 5X optical zoom, and a new 48MP wide camera with upgraded light sensitivity.

Where to preorder the Pixel Watch 5

The updated Pixel Watch 5 comes in two sizes, with the 41mm model starting at $399, and the larger 45mm model starting at $429. In addition to faster processing and more memory, there are a variety of new features for exercising, like a workout builder, and a more accurate GPS in crowded areas. The watch adds a variety of new long-term health features under the umbrella of “Health Guardian” which can detect some medical emergencies, watch blood pressure trends, and keep track of insulin resistance.

Carrier offers and promotions

AT&T is offering a variety of discounts if you want to upgrade to the new phones or the Pixel Watch 5. Most notably, you can get a Pixel 11 Pro for free via 36 months of credits if you trade in a Pixel phone of any year or condition, although you’ll need to keep the service active for the duration and have a service of at least $80 a month. The same deal is available for a Pixel 11 Pro XL with qualified trade-ins. If you’re starting a new line and buying a device that’s $500 or more with an installment plan, you can also claim 50 percent off a Pixel Watch 5.

Update, August 12th: Added additional deal details.

Tech.title: Twitch streamers can now opt out from training Amazon’s AI
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Twitch users can now opt out of allowing their content to be used to train Amazon’s generative AI models. Opting out means that “your streams, VODs, clips, stream chats, and pictures and text on your channel” won’t be used in “future training” of an Amazon AI model “whose purpose is to generate or synthesize text, audio, images, or video,” according to a Twitch support page.

Other “AI-supported” features like captions and safety tools will still function if you opt-out of generative AI training. However, if you participate in a chat on another person’s stream, “their opt-out preferences govern if that chat can be used for training,” Twitch says.

The “Training for Generative AI” toggle is present for me in Twitch’s settings under the Security and Privacy tab. It was toggled on when I found it, and I’ve asked Amazon if that’s the default.

Here’s the full text of Amazon’s description for the toggle:

Allow your channel content to train generative AI content models at Amazon. Turning this off does not opt you out of Twitch and Amazon using your channel content for other purposes described in the Twitch Privacy Notice, including using AI-supported Twitch features that benefit the community by facilitating streamer growth and monetization (such as real-time sponsorship campaign assistance), viewer discovery (such as recommendations), and community safety (such as AutoMod). Learn more

Tech.title: How Google’s new Pixel 11 phones compare to last year’s models
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google just added four new phones to the Pixel family: the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. They’re slightly more expensive than their predecessors, but they come with some notable upgrades, including improved cameras and a new Tensor G6 chip that should deliver faster performance. The phones also have new photography tools, like Magic Capture, along with improvements to Gemini Intelligence, expanded Live Translate capabilities, and the ability to use Circle to Search directly through the camera.

To make deciding whether you’ll upgrade or hold onto your last-gen phone a little simpler, we’re focusing on comparing the specs of the 6.3-inch Pixel 11 and Pixel 10 models, as well as the 6.8-inch Pro XL models. If you’re curious about how the Pixel 11 Pro Fold compares to its predecessor (and to the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 series foldables), we’ve got a spec comparison right here.

Before we get to the specs, here’s a breakdown of what’s new.

They’re more expensive, but you get more storage

The most obvious difference is that, like almost everything these days, they’re more expensive than before. The Pixel 11 starts at $899, $100 more than its predecessor, but Google has doubled the base storage to 256GB with 12GB of RAM. The Pixel 11 Pro starts at $1,099 — $100 more than the Pixel 10 Pro’s launch price — with the same 256GB of storage and 12GB of RAM, and is available with up to 1TB of storage and 16GB of RAM. Meanwhile, Google’s larger 6.8-inch Pixel 11 Pro XL starts at $1,299 and offers the same storage and RAM configurations as the Pro.

Tensor G6 allows for even more AI features

Both the Pixel 11 and Pro phones run on Google’s new Tensor G6 chip, which the company claims should improve performance by up to 25 percent compared to its predecessor. The new chip also powers a host of AI upgrades, including improvements to Gemini Intelligence, which Google says can now pull more context from supported apps to proactively surface useful information. There are also new voice-to-text tools that remove filler words and clean up formatting, while writing assistance can use what’s on your screen to help draft, rewrite, and refine messages. Live Translate is also available on videos, podcasts, and voice messages, and Circle to Search now works directly through the camera, letting you identify objects, translate text, or search your surroundings without snapping a photo first.

The cameras get some notable upgrades inside and out

There are a number of camera improvements, too, along with new photography and video features. On the hardware side, the Pixel 11 has a slimmer camera bar that sits flush when paired with one of Google’s phone cases. It can also zoom in farther than its predecessor, reaching up to 30x for photos, while the Pixel 11 Pro series gets an updated 1/1.3-inch 50-megapixel sensor for its main camera and a redesigned telephoto sensor that Google says captures 32 percent more light. The Pro can also zoom up to 120x and features a 42-megapixel selfie camera. The Pro should be quicker at shooting in the dark, too, with Google claiming its Instant Night Sight can capture photos up to 4.5 times faster.

Google has made several software improvements as well. The new Magic Capture mode in the camera app automatically captures photos and videos to make them ready to share with a tap. Camera Looks let you create custom styles for photos, while the Pixel 11 Pro series can record stabilized video at up to 8K using Pro Stable Video with Video Boost. A new Creator Suite also features tools for trimming and rearranging clips, using a teleprompter while recording, and improving speech clarity, and it automatically saves clips to a designated project album.

How the Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 compare

Those are some of the biggest changes, but they’re far from the only differences between the two lineups. For example, both the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro offer an Extreme Charging Mode that prioritizes charging over other tasks for a faster boost when you’re short on time. The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL also gets HiLight, colored LEDs around the camera flash that can alert you to things, like calls when your phone is face down or when Gemini is activated.

Tech.title: Northrop’s robot space mechanic is a new way to keep satellites at work longer
Tech.content:
High above the Earth, a new generation of robots designed to keep satellites working longer is replacing its predecessor — quite literally.

This week, a spacecraft built and operated by Northrop Grumman called a Mission Extension Vehicle (MEV) unplugged from a communications satellite operated by the Australian firm Optus. For more than a year, the MEV spacecraft has been stuck to the back of the Optus satellite, keeping it in the right place in space so it can continue its mission.

Now, the satellite life-extension spacecraft is leaving to make room for its replacement. In July, four new Northrop spacecraft launched into orbit on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. One is called the Mission Robotic Vehicle (MRV), a powerful satellite equipped with two advanced robotic arms that was developed by DARPA, the U.S. military research organization. The other three are called Mission Extension Pods, or MEPs, smaller, simpler satellites that are essentially modular propulsion systems.

Those four spacecraft are currently headed for targets around 27,000 miles above the Earth. In 2027, the MRV will use its robotic arms to attach one of the MEP pods to the Optus satellite, which should keep it in orbit for years to come.

The satellites that provide communications or scan the planet with various sensors only last for so long. They typically fail when they run out of fuel to stay in the right place, not because their computers and transceivers stop working. The Optus satellite was launched in 2009, and designed for a 15-year lifespan. If all goes well, the satellite could fly — and generate revenue — for another six years.

Now, cheaper launch costs and lower-cost space components are making spacecraft repair missions a reality.

The goal is “a paradigm shift where we can see space as sustainable, with a more resilient architecture and infrastructure base where we can do things like spacecraft repairs, life extension, or even upgrades and maintenance of satellites,” according to Northrop’s director of logistics and servicing, Cassie Wong.

There are two MEVs in orbit right now, launched in 2019 and 2020, which have provided 10 years of life extension to three customers, including two different Intelsat spacecraft and the Optus satellite. MEV-1 will wait in a parking orbit for another customer, while MEV-2 is currently attached to its Intelsat customer until 2030.

The Mission Robotic Vehicle, or MRV, represents an evolution of the business model. Satellite operators buy and own the MEPs, which are permanently attached to their spacecraft. That frees up the MRV to service more vehicles, creating a cheaper offering.

The offering requires some serious technology chops. The vehicles need to autonomously approach one another and dock safely, not a simple task when both are moving at velocities of thousands of miles an hour. The MEVs use a docking probe to plug in and hang onto satellite thruster nozzles. Meanwhile, the MRVs will need to carefully attach the MEPs using their robotic arms.

Unlike most satellites, the MRV is designed to be refueled in orbit — in part, a proof of concept for the kind of capabilities other satellites will need if this kind of in-orbit servicing becomes a norm. Right now, the extra cost and weight of such adaptations keeps spacecraft operators from investing in them.

Indeed, the current trend in satellites is flying lots of cheap, effectively replaceable spacecraft in low orbits, as Starlink and Amazon LEO do. On the other hand, spacecraft keep getting bigger, and there are plenty of expensive, large satellites in orbit that could benefit from life extension. Wong hopes that the MRV will take on other missions in the future, adding new components to satellites as well as adjusting their orbits.

That’s likely to include defense customers, given the number of expensive satellites it owns in high orbits, and DARPA’s involvement in developing the MRV’s arms. Indeed, the U.S. Space Force has previously characterized a Chinese servicing spacecraft with robotic arms as a weapon, since it could theoretically grapple and degrade a rival satellite. Northrop says that its vehicles are focused on servicing missions.

The vehicle could also be used in LEO, Wong says, to extend the life with valuable assets there. The startup Katalyst Space is attempting a similar mission to extend the life of a NASA space telescope after malfunctions left its vehicle tumbling last month. The company has a fix in place and hopes to complete the mission.

Tech.title: Amazon will train on Twitch streamers’ content by default, unless they opt out
Tech.content:
The streaming platform Twitch will now use creators’ content to help train generative AI models for its parent company, Amazon. This move has inspired swift and concentrated backlash from the Twitch community, especially because creators are opted in to having their content used for this AI training by default.

For Amazon, these stream recordings are incredibly valuable, offering thousands of hours of audio and video content to help train AI models. But Twitch users worry that since creators have to manually opt out, they might be surrendering their content to train Amazon’s AI content models without even knowing it. This is especially concerning on a platform like Twitch, where creators are often recording livestreams of themselves and their voices for many hours per week.

Image Credits:Twitch /

In a stream on the official Twitch channel, Twitch Head of Community Mary Kish and Chief Product Officer Mike Minton addressed a live audience of nearly 3,000 aggrieved users, many of whom were posting anti-AI sentiments in the chat.

“Why is it not opt-in? That’s what everybody is spamming in chat. I get it. ‘Let me opt in versus making me opt out,’” Minton said. “Well, there’s an honest answer… If this was opt-in, nobody would opt in. That’s honestly the answer.”

Twitch knows that its community of streamers is largely opposed to the use of generative AI, since the most prevalent generative AI products are trained on books, images, videos, and other materials scraped from the internet without consent.

Even Twitch’s approach to breaking this news shows that the company is braced for backlash. Instead of telling the community that Amazon would begin training on Twitch users’ content, Twitch framed this change as “[adding] a setting that lets you opt out of having your channel content used to train generative AI content models across Amazon.”

In some cases, this created confusion among streamers about whether their content had already been fed to Amazon without their knowledge. When one user asked if their videos had already been used for training, Minton responded, “I don’t actually know the answer to that question because I don’t know what Amazon […] has done in terms of model training and what they’ve used and not used.”

Kish noted that Twitch is not unique in its use of user content for AI training. Meta, for example, uses public content from its platforms to train its own AI models, meaning that if your Facebook and Instagram accounts are public, then your data has probably already been used for Meta’s AI training. (If you live in the U.K., you can opt out of Meta’s training — if not, the only way to “opt out” is to use private settings, which isn’t feasible for creators who monetize their accounts.)

Kish said that even including an opt-out option on Twitch is “a reflection of reacting to this community’s voice that you are not wanting to train Gen AI models, and we want to give you that option.”

To opt out of AI training on Twitch, users can navigate to their channel settings (not the creator dashboard), select the security and privacy tab, scroll down to the option “training for generative AI,” and toggle it off.

Tech.title: Grubhub’s $24M FTC settlement is finally reaching diners and drivers
Tech.content:
Well over half a million Grubhub drivers and customers are set to receive a share of $23.8 million following allegations that the food delivery company misled workers about their potential earnings and engaged in other deceptive practices.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) announced on Wednesday that it’s distributing the money to 640,038 consumers, with most recipients receiving a check in the mail. Some will receive their payments through PayPal.

The payouts stem from a lawsuit the FTC and Illinois attorney general filed against Grubhub in December 2024. The complaint accused the company of a range of unlawful practices, including making misleading claims about how much drivers could earn, restricting customers’ access to their accounts and money, and listing restaurants on its platform without their permission.
